Support us <https://email.mgeu.euobserver.com/c/eJyMkc1yrCAQRp8GdneKHxFdsLhVU74GhU2rJIIGcZK8fcrJTCWZRSrbbk53f4feFZhs8EaLpqKwpIJvxeC-9BvmC-Z_3oX5_SSUYFVLvVGAtaZouG6VrrlkDZ1My533DfBhGNB71njRejagZorVvRNAg8kYVxtdmDFbr12rBvD2NoQLRioWR9xPX4tPsET6tPSft2lNZzOVsm5E_ieiI6JzAMueygNCRBcx9pi3KaxEdrlEC3OAZyLPSnkO2AAR9VHelj0DEnl-THvrR_Rhj0f_uPtWBBdXF8b0A7NxySmk0e6rdwWtaDgXtWVVfrljh9hUiDxfPR8D7YbJYz7yMVC16Bt-98Fbmk3C123GUjDzSsqWVGw8sKuX7z_0y3JaMK6zK_jH5xcjPgIAAP__wqiyUw>

Good morning.

Budget talks in Brussels are expected to run late on Thursday (26 November) as EU leaders clash over how big the next seven-year budget should be, who foots the bill and whether all 27 must pay for Ukraine – with time running short to reach a deal before the end of the year.

On the table is a nearly €2 trillion budget for 2028-2034. But no deal was really ever expected to come out of this special European Council.

In line with an unspoken Brussels tradition, EU Council president António Costa knew he needed a ‘bad’ summit before a ‘good’ one would even be possible...

Merz und der EU-Gipfel: Scheitern mit Ansage

Präsentiert von YouTube Von HANS VON DER BURCHARD Mit FERDINAND KNAPP PRÄSENTIERT VON Schicken Sie uns Ihre Tipps hier oder hier | X @vonderburchard @

Präsentiert von YouTube

Von HANS VON DER BURCHARD

Mit FERDINAND KNAPP

PRÄSENTIERT VON

Schicken Sie uns Ihre Tipps hier oder hier | X @vonderburchard @R_Buchsteiner | Das Playbook anhören oder online lesen

Moin Berlin, hier schreibt Hans von der Burchard.

Gestern Abend kurz nach Mitternacht war Schluss: Der EU-Sondergipfel zum Haushalt, der eigentlich noch bis heute Nachmittag dauern sollte, endete nach nur einem Tag. Was dies bedeutet, analysiere ich gleich.

Außerdem bei uns: Friedrich Merz glaubt weiterhin an eine Renteneinigung vor Weihnachten, erneute Verzögerung beim Bundestagsbau in der Neustädtischen Kirchstraße und der Streit des BSW um den Umgang mit der AfD.

Hörtipps: Am Samstag spricht Gordon beim Spaziergang mit Markus Frohnmaier über die außenpolitische Ausrichtung der AfD. Im Security Sunday mit Rixa Fürsen geht es dann um die Verteidigungsausgaben der EU: Rund 500 Mrd. Euro investieren die Staaten pro Jahr, doch wirklich effektiv wird dieses Geld nicht eingesetzt, kritisiert der Ökonom Moritz Schularick.

**(Anzeige) Eine Nachricht von YouTube: Digitale Bildung für alle: Im Juni 2026 schauten über 25 Millionen monatlich aktive Zuschauer*innen in Deutschland akademische Videos. Laut Oxford Economics setzen zudem 90 % der YouTube nutzenden Lehrkräfte Videos direkt im Unterricht ein. Mehr zum gesellschaftlichen Beitrag von YouTube hier.**

SEITE EINS

RÜCKSCHLAG: Eine ausbleibende Einigung war zwar erwartet worden, doch das Scheitern des EU-Haushaltsgipfels gestern Abend war besonders krachend.

Anflug von Pessimismus: „Ich bin mir nicht sicher, dass eine Einigung noch bis Jahresende gelingt“, sagte Merz am Abend. „Aber ich gebe die Hoffnung nicht auf.“

Macron warnt: Falls die weiteren Gespräche in den nächsten Wochen scheitern sollten, müsse die EU bis nach den französischen Wahlen im Mai warten und womöglich mit Marine Le Pen verhandeln. Denn ein Strecken der Verhandlungen bis in den Januar sei „demokratisch nicht möglich“, da man zu nahe an die Präsidentschaftswahlen gerate.

Macron wird für Merz aber auch zum Sorgenfaktor: Er besteht auf hohe Agrarzahlungen und erschwert damit eine Einigung. Gestern zwang eine vorgezogene Pressekonferenz des französischen Präsidenten auch Merz dazu, früher als geplant vor die Presse zu treten. Trotz vieler Zweiergespräche ziehen die beiden noch nicht am selben Strang.

Verlierer des Abends: António Costa. Die Kritik an der Verhandlungsführung des EU-Ratspräsidenten mehrt sich; Schwedens Premier boykottierte gar ein Treffen mit ihm. In den nächsten Wochen wird sich zeigen, ob er die Federführung bei den Gesprächen behält.

In früheren Zeiten hätte jetzt Angela Merkel übernommen. Ob Merz das kann?

Immerhin etwas gelernt: Ganz nutzlos war der Gipfel nicht, meint der österreichische Kanzler. „Ich glaube, dass —, auch wenn wir uns heute scheinbar nicht aufeinander zubewegen konnten, — nun wissen, was notwendig ist, damit es beim nächsten Mal gelingen kann“, sagte Christian Stocker.

In drei Wochen, am 17. Dezember, beginnt der nächste Gipfel, der sich bis ins Wochenende strecken könnte. Eine Kraftprobe für den deutschen Kanzler, der kurz zuvor auch noch zum G20-Gipfel nach Miami muss.

Immerhin: „Weihnachten wollen wir alle zu Hause sein“, so Merz.

Meine Prognose: Ganz so schlecht stehen die Chancen auf eine Einigung nicht. Gestern gab es vor allem viel Theater und Pokerspiele. In drei Wochen werden alle Seiten deutlichen Einigungsdruck spüren — denn niemand will mit Le Pen verhandeln müssen.

Zumal dann das Risiko bestünde, dass wegen der Verzögerungen zum Start der nächsten Haushaltsperiode noch keine Gelder fließen können.

Noch eine Blockade: Ungarn, die Slowakei und Tschechien bleiben bei ihrer Weigerung, sich an der finanziellen Absicherung des 45-Milliarden-EU-Kredits für die Ukraine zu beteiligen.

Bulgarien zeigt sich offen für einen Kompromiss, bei dem nur die Kosten für die nichtmilitärischen Teile des Kredits übernommen würden. Merz sieht „Hinweise“ dafür, dass auf diese Weise die Widerstände überwunden werden könnten.

DIPLOMATISCHE DEPESCHE

BRAVO, TRUMP: „Mit großer Freude“ reagierte Merz unterdessen auf Trumps Aufforderung an Putin, „alle militärischen Aggressionen“ gegen Europa einzustellen. „Das ist gut, dass er das tut. Damit nimmt er eine klare Position, die wir alle teilen“, sagte der Kanzler am Abend.

Wahr ist aber auch: Trump singt oft das Lied desjenigen, den er zuletzt getroffen hat. Und das war gerade NATO-Chef Mark Rutte. Nachdem sich der US-Präsident zuletzt mit Putin getroffen hatte, nannte er diesen noch tagelang seinen „Freund“.

Artikel-5-Irgendwas: Auf meine Frage, ob die derzeit viel diskutierten „Artikel-5-ähnlichen“ Sicherheitsgarantien auch amerikanische Truppen in der Ukraine enthalten sollten, um einen Frieden gegen befürchtete erneute russische Aggressionen abzusichern, wich Merz aus: „Wie das im Einzelnen konkret aussieht, darüber zu sprechen ist heute viel zu früh.“

Anzeige

FRAKTIONSEBENE

RENTEN-VORWEIHNACHTSZEIT: Bis in den Abend tagte gestern die Verhandlungsrunde um Alexander Schweitzer, Nina Warken, Alexander Dobrindt und Björn Böhning, um im Rentenstreit einem Kompromiss näherzukommen. Ausgang: unklar.

Aber gab es da nicht einen Vorschlag? Das Kompromiss-Konzept von Johannes Winkel, Pascal Reddig und Marc Biadacz wird in der SPD abgelehnt. Dort ist man mittlerweile der Meinung, die Rente mit 63 ganz beibehalten zu wollen — anders als noch im Sommer von der Alterssicherungskommission vorgeschlagen.

Zähe Gespräche: Die Idee der Respekt-Rente sollte „etwas Bewegung“ in die festgefahrenen Gespräche bringen, sagt Pascal Reddig im 200-Sekunden-Interview. Er beklagt, dass alle in ihren „ideologischen Schützengräben“ säßen und mit dieser Blockadehaltung auch die guten Dinge wie die Kapitalrente gefährdeten.

Es wird Zeit: Bei der gesamten Rentendebatte „haben wir leider fünf Monate verplempert“, kritisiert der CDU-Politiker. Jetzt müsse man eine Lösung finden und „umsetzen, was wir angekündigt haben“. Am Ende hänge auch der „Erfolg der Koalition“ von der Rentenfrage ab.

Interessant: Nicht alle in der Unionsfraktion waren vom neuen Renten-Vorstoß begeistert. In der Arbeitsgruppe Arbeit und Soziales fühlten sich einige übergangen. Alle Details zum Streit lesen Sie in der Analyse von Rasmus Buchsteiner, Nikolaus Doll und Maximilian Heimerzheim.

Tik-Tak: „Wir kommen gut voran. Der Kanzler hat mir gesagt, vor Weihnachten sollen wir möglichst fertig sein“, sagte Schweitzer gestern Abend bei der Chemie- und Pharmaindustrie, wie Romanus Otte berichtet.

Ach ja: „Ich freue mich übrigens auch über alle aktuellen Vorschläge, die deutlich machen, was auf allen Seiten in Bewegung geraten ist“, so der Arbeitsminister weiter.

Auch der Kanzler will das Gesetz vor Weihnachten im Kabinett beschließen. Angepeilt ist die Sitzung am 9. Dezember; auch eine Woche später wäre noch möglich. Merz und Lars Klingbeil wissen, dass sich daran auch die Zukunft der Koalition entscheidet.

PRÄSIDIALEBENE

SCHLECHTE NACHRICHTEN FÜR DEN BUNDESTAG: Die frühere US-Botschaft in der Neustädtischen Kirchstraße, zwischen Einstein und Il Punto, wird seit Jahren für die Parlamentsverwaltung hergerichtet.

Der Bau sollte eigentlich 2018 übergeben werden, doch dann verzögerte sich alles. Zuletzt wurde eine Übergabe im Oktober 2027 angepeilt. Wird aber wieder nichts, berichtet Rasmus Buchsteiner.

Konkret: In der Sitzung der Bundestags-Baukommission am Mittwoch gab es die Ankündigung, dass sich alles um ein weiteres Jahr verzögert — bis zum Herbst 2028 also.

Noch was: Die Herrichtung des Renaissancebau wird teurer. Die Kosten steigen um 1,2 Millionen auf knapp 127,6 Millionen Euro. Ursprünglich kalkuliert waren 50,6 Millionen Euro.

PARTEIEN

AFD-STREIT BEIM BSW: Heute und morgen trifft sich das BSW (neuerdings: Bündnis Soziale Gerechtigkeit und Wirtschaftliche Vernunft) zum Parteitag in Dresden. Dabei wird sich vieles um die AfD drehen — oder besser gesagt der Umgang mit ihr, berichtet Ferdinand.

Schwieriger Spagat: Das BSW will sich weder dem Lager der „Altparteien“ noch Brandmauer-Logiken unterordnen.

Wie hältst du’s mit den Rechten? In Sachsen-Anhalt, wo BSW-Abgeordnete für den AfDler Tobias Rausch als Landtagspräsidenten gestimmt haben, setzt man auf sachbezogene Zusammenarbeit mit Rechtsaußen, etwa durch gemeinsame Anträge und Absprachen.

Rote Linien zieht man dagegen bei einer Koalition mit der AfD und bei der Wahl von Ulrich Siegmund zum Ministerpräsidenten: Da will sich das BSW enthalten. Der Landesverband nennt seinen Kurs den „Magdeburger Weg“.

Ost-West-Konflikt? Einige in der Partei — darunter fünf westdeutsche Mitglieder des Bundesvorstands wie Christian Leye und Klaus Ernst — sehen darin eine zu starke Annäherung. Ein Antrag von rund 200 Mitgliedern fordert, längerfristige Absprachen mit der AfD auszuschließen.

Die Parteispitze bemüht sich um einen Kompromiss: Parteichef Fabio De Masi hat einen Vorschlag zur Ergänzung des Leitantrags vorgelegt, über den am Wochenende abgestimmt werden soll. Er hält am Kern des Magdeburger Wegs fest.

Strategische Entscheidungen, etwa über einen Haushalt, sollen laut De Masi mit dem Präsidium abgestimmt werden — dem ja auch mehrere Kritiker angehören. Sahra Wagenknecht unterstützt De Masis Vorstoß.

Das wird schon: Die Befürworter sind optimistisch, dass der Leitantrag durchgeht.

Und wenn nicht? Unklar. In Sachsen-Anhalt will man jedoch am „Magdeburger Weg“ festhalten und sich nicht reinreden lassen.

Die Leiden des jungen BSW: Im Hinterkopf einiger dürfte noch stecken, dass unter anderem der Streit um den Umgang mit den etablierten Parteien und der AfD in Thüringen zum Bruch der BSW-Landtagsfraktion beigetragen hatte, die dort mit CDU und SPD regierte.

LÄNDERPUNKTE

SIEGMUND VERHINDERN? Nach Infos von T-Online fand gestern Abend erstmals ein Treffen zwischen BSW, SPD, Grünen, Linken und CDU statt, um für die Ministerpräsidentenwahl am 8. Dezember einen überparteilichen Kandidaten zu finden.

Verflixt: Die Suche nach einem gemeinsamen Kandidaten von fünf (!) Parteien wird schwierig: Die CDU-Fraktion ist zerstritten, das BSW verhandelt mit der AfD und auch der rot-grün-rote Block ist sich überhaupt nicht einig.

Kompromissversuch: Cedric Looks hört, dass die SPD inzwischen einen Kandidaten hat, mit dem zumindest auch die CDU mitgehen würde.

BAND DES BUNDES

DER KAMERA-VORSTOSS: Das Innenministerium prüft verstärkte Video- und Sensorüberwachung, um kritische Infrastruktur besser vor Sabotage, Spionage, Diebstahl und anderen Angriffen zu schützen. Das teilte ein Sprecher auf Anfrage von Joana Lehner zu den neuen Bundesratsforderungen mit.

Der Länder-Wunsch: Hintergrund ist eine Entschließung des Bundesrats auf Initiative von Nordrhein-Westfalen. Die Länder verlangen Videoüberwachung auch im direkten Umfeld der Anlagen, und zwar nicht erst bei konkreten Hinweisen auf einen Anschlag.

Der Paragrafen-Knoten: Dafür soll das KRITIS (Kritische Infrastrukturen)-Dachgesetz konkretisiert werden, denn Unternehmen fehlt darin bislang die Rechtssicherheit dafür. Warum das so ist und wie das BMI darauf blickt, lesen Sie in unserem Pro Energie und Klima.

SPOTTED

AUF DIE PRESSE: Beim Medientreff der MVFP-Landesvertretung Berlin-Brandenburg in der Austernbank gesichtet: Christian Wulff, Johann Wadephul, Kai Wegner, Matthias Miersch, Rolf Mützenich, Ralf Stegner, Thomas Bareiß, Israels Botschafter Ron Prosor, Hubertus Heil, Franziska Giffey, Felor Badenberg, Diana Zimmermann, Stefan Aust und Georg Mascolo. BEIM PARLAMENTARISCHEN ABEND DER CHEMIE- UND PHARMAINDUSTRIE waren Alexander Schweitzer, Steffen Bilger, die Chefs von Covestro und BASF, Markus Steilemann und Markus Kamieth, IGBCE-Chef Michael Vassiliadis sowie Ex-FDP-Chef Christian Dürr.

AGENDA

— Die Regierungspressekonferenz findet um 11:30 Uhr statt.

— Anglermesse: Um 9 Uhr macht Alois Rainer einen Eröffnungsrundgang auf der Angelwelt.

— Bildung: Um 16:45 Uhr nimmt Karin Prien an der Strategiediskussion auf der Fachtagung „25 Jahre PISA — Weltweite und nationale Entwicklungen: Was ist zu tun?“ teil.

— Haushaltsfinale: Am letzten Sitzungstag in diesem Monat beginnt der Bundestag ab 12:40 Uhr mit der Schlussdebatte zum Haushaltsgesetz 2027 und stimmt anschließend namentlich darüber ab.

🗞️ Not dead in the water

27 November 2026 | Daily newsletter

͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌

Good morning,

Just yesterday I was discussing with some friends how very similar we humans are to parasites. Take us off the face of the earth, and chances are the planet will return to a naturally balanced state. Fortunately, there are some humans that dedicate their lives to restoring natural habitats. In this week's long read, Liene Lūsīte and Guillaume Amouret went to meet some of them restoring Denmark's Vejle Fjord.

Claire Brown

Editor

Nature restoration

“With a bait like that, you could catch a trout!” I'm standing waist-deep in cold water, fishing rod in hand, while Kaare Manniche Ebert teaches me the basics of fishing. Under the overcast sky, the fjord takes on greyish shades. But something in the water is off: with every step, it clouds and darkens. The murky fjord is struggling to breathe.

Guillaume Amouret, Liene Lūsīte

What it takes to restore a fjord

Two years after its symbolic burial, life is very slowly returning to Denmark's Vejle Fjord.

〉 Read article 〉 Hide again

Kaare Manniche Ebert stands on a wooden jetty, scanning the water for clumps of eelgrass. Then he wades in, gently sweeps his fishing net past one growing on the sandy bottom, and pulls out two little grey shrimp and a few shellfish.

“Life has come back, but it's still not convincing,” he says.

Ebert is a fish biologist and has been an adviser to the Danish Sports Fishing Association for about 30 years. Over the decades, he has watched life slowly disappear from Vejle Fjord.

Situated on Denmark's Jutland peninsula, about a three-hour drive west of Copenhagen, the fjord has become a focal point in the debate over nitrogen pollution in Denmark – and across Europe.

“Just 15 years ago, sea trout used to stay here the entire year because there was a lot of food for them. There used to be big sand worms swimming around in the water,” Ebert recalls.

This year, he has only fished in the fjord twice. “To catch a sea trout, I have to fish for about ten hours. That's a lot of work for one fish.”

Two years ago, Ebert says, he couldn't find any life among the eelgrass. Shrimp and various species of small fish are now present again. But the fjord is far from recovered. Brownish slime covers the once-green eelgrass: “fedtemøg”, as the Danes call it, or greasy muck.

Vejle Fjord suffers from eutrophication: a process in which excess nutrients in the water, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, feed the brown algae. These cloud the water, blocking sunlight from the underwater plants. Without enough light, eelgrass can't produce oxygen through photosynthesis. As the algae decompose, they consume oxygen, too.

Warm, calm weather makes the problem worse. Warmer water holds less oxygen, while the absence of wind means less mixing with oxygen-rich surface water. Fish may swim away, but slower, less mobile animals can suffocate.

Other Danish fjords are in even worse condition. A recent report by Aarhus University found little or no oxygen in the bottom waters of outer Aabenraa Fjord from June to October, and in inner Flensburg Fjord since mid-May.

In 2024, Ebert's association and Greenpeace held a symbolic burial of the fjord to raise awareness of oxygen depletion. Around 1,000 people gathered at the local open-air amphitheatre on its shore. “The idea was not only to mourn the fjord, but also to give hope that nature can come back if we do something about it,” explains Ebert.

Two years later, we went there to see for ourselves what had changed.

Eelgrass from the Vejle Fjord. Photo courtesy of Guillaume Amouret, 2026

Putting the habitat back

Rune Christian Husted Steinfurth is a coastal marine ecologist at the University of Southern Denmark. He works on Sund Vejle Fjord, a restoration project launched in 2020 to restore damaged habitats, including eelgrass meadows, mussel beds, and boulder reefs.

Pollution is only part of the damage, he tells us. Fishers harvested blue mussels from the seabed, while boats hauled boulders off the fjord floor for use in on-land construction. An estimated 8.3 million cubic metres of stone were removed from Danish waters during the 20th century (about 3,300 Olympic-sized swimming pools).

Since 2020, the restoration project has established six hectares of eelgrass, 52 hectares of mussel beds, and eight hectares of stone reefs, according to Vejle municipality. At some sites, eelgrass is now spreading without further planting.

“We have planted about 120,000 plants, and they have now expanded to more than four million plants,” estimates Steinfurth. “So it’s really working.”

He stresses that these were carefully selected sites. Elsewhere, conditions remain too poor for planting.

Mussel beds should eventually replenish themselves, too, but too few young mussels are surviving. Green crabs eat them, and both Steinfurth and Ebert suspect that the crabs are flourishing because the larger predators that would normally eat them have disappeared.

“Since cod and eels left the fjord, crabs are thriving here,” says Ebert, pointing to broken crab shells on the jetty. Seagulls are now their only natural predators, so humans are stepping in to help. “Fishers catch them and supply restaurants, or sell them to be processed into animal feed,” he explains.

But removing 20 tonnes a year for two years made no measurable difference. More crabs kept arriving, says Steinfurth. The team is now working on the assumption that if they restore the habitat, the animals will follow.

From field to fjord

The pollution problem begins on land. Agriculture accounts for about 70% of Denmark's land-based nitrogen discharges into the sea, while about 60% of the country's land is farmland.

Of the crops grown in Denmark, 85% go to animal feed, supporting a livestock industry heavily focused on pig farming. The resulting manure, rich in nitrogen, is spread across fields as fertiliser.

Crops cannot absorb all the nitrogen applied to the soil. The excess can wash into rivers and fjords. Much of Denmark's farmland was once too wet to cultivate, so farmers have spent generations draining their fields through ditches and underground pipes. This “has created a very fast route for the nutrients from the fields to the rivers, lakes, and estuaries,” explains Steinfurth.

Once in the fjord, nitrogen feeds the algae that choke the ecosystem. This limits what restoration projects alone can achieve. Reducing pollution nationally is therefore crucial, Emil Bejer-Pedersen, campaign manager at Greenpeace Denmark, told us. “These efforts are not going to get the whole fjord back in a good ecological state, but they are definitely a helping hand.”

Denmark has reduced agricultural pollution before. A study of five river valleys between 1990 and 2018 found that nitrogen runoff had fallen by 30-52%, largely thanks to national regulations. These included restrictions on fertiliser use, stricter manure management, and requirements for farmers to grow crops that absorb leftover nitrogen between harvests.

Restricting fertiliser use is one way to tackle the problem; changing how land is managed is another. Around Vejle, this has been happening for years. Sections of the Vejle river that had previously been straightened have been given their bends back, while wetlands have also been brought back. This slows the flow of water and gives nature time to filter out nitrogen before it reaches the fjord.

Taking farmland out of production altogether would reduce pollution at its source. That is one of the aims of Denmark's historic Green Tripartite Agreement, signed in 2024 by the government, farming organisations, and environmental groups.

The agreement aims to reshape Denmark's landscape, returning around a tenth of the country's land to forests and natural habitats by 2045. It includes taking 140,000 hectares of carbon-rich farmland and surrounding land out of production by 2030 – an area roughly the size of the Faroe Islands.

As part of the deal, Denmark has committed to reducing nitrogen discharges into its coastal waters by 14,800 tonnes. The main approach is to change how land is used: farmers are encouraged to reduce fertiliser use and convert their farmland into forests, wetlands, and natural areas.

But transforming farmland takes years, and farmers' participation is voluntary. So the agreement came with a backstop, dubbed the “ nitrogen hammer”. Wherever the required cuts in nitrogen emission are not achieved, binding limits on farms are intended to make up for the shortfall.

Denmark decided to go a step further and passed a new law in September and it is due to take effect in January 2027. From then on, each farm will have a quota limiting how much nitrogen can leak from its fields into waterways. The restrictions are meant to be temporary, easing as more farmland is converted.

Farmers on the edge

Nis Kristian Hjort, president of Vejle’s farmer union, agrees with the green tripartite's approach: “We have a responsibility to be aware of those negative aspects of farming.”

He farms about 100 hectares on fjord's southern bank. Until recently, he was a dairy farmer. Like much of Denmark's agricultural land, his fields are used to grow animal feed. He sold his 120 cows to a younger neighbour, but continues to grow feed crops.

He also took part in the discussions surrounding Sund Vejle Fjord and supported the restoration project. “About one year ago we agreed on the farmland we could leave out to nature. Farmers were ready to move along with the green transition.”

But the new nitrogen rules will hit some farmers harder than others, depending on how much nitrogen is expected to leak from their fields into waterways. This largely comes down to how close they are to a river or lake.

“Less fertiliser means lower yields; the land loses its value,” Hjort explained. “That comes on top of giving up some land, and will bring some farmers into financial difficulties.”

Beyond Denmark

Water from Vejle Fjord eventually ends up in the Baltic Sea. In 2023, the land draining into the Danish straits, where the fjord lies, released more than three times as much nitrogen per square kilometre as the Baltic Sea average, according to HELCOM, the organisation monitoring the sea's health. It linked the high levels to intensive farming and a dense population.

The problem extends far beyond Denmark. According to the European Environment Agency, only 38% of EU's surface waters are currently in good ecological health. The EU’s Water Framework Directive requires member states to bring their waters to good ecological status. This means meaning healthy populations of aquatic plants and animals, while also meeting limits on chemical pollution.

The original deadline was 2015, but countries were allowed to extend it to 2027 under certain conditions, including technical difficulties, disproportionate costs, and slow natural recovery. The Nature Restoration Regulation adds further obligations to repair damaged habitats, including seagrass beds.

Denmark will miss the 2027 deadline too, says Steinfurth. “We will not make it by next year.” The problem is the enforcement, he argues. “I think this comes down to not only having these laws and regulations, but also enforcing them. And if member states don’t oblige, then they need to find a way to make them responsible,” he said.

Asked what other countries could learn from Denmark, a Commission official pointed to the cooperation between government, farmers’ organisations, and environmental groups, like in the Green Tripartite Agreement. Farmers and landowners must be treated “not as passive recipients of obligations, but as active partners in implementation,” the official told us.

The Commission also wants to help farmers finance the transition. Under its proposal for the next Common Agricultural Policy, farms could receive up to €200,000 to cover the costs and risks of moving to more sustainable practices.

How long does a fjord need?

Back on the jetty, Ebert observes the water. It looks a little clearer, with less brown algae than in previous years. “It might be because we had less rain this summer,” he says.

The latest Aarhus University report on oxygen depletion in Danish waters supports this observation: with less rain this year, less water ran off the land, carrying fewer nutrients into the sea. But for Ebert, this is another reason Denmark must continue reducing nitrogen pollution from farmland. “With higher temperatures, the production of brown algae will increase, and so will the risk of oxygen depletion,” he warns.

Even with less nitrogen, a fjord doesn't regenerate overnight. Some muddy sediments could take 50 years to recover naturally, even if all nutrient pollution stopped, Steinfurth said. “There are Danish experts that say more than 100 years, but it’s models and assumptions, right? It all depends on what actions are being taken along the road.”

For now, his team continues to monitor the eelgrass as it spreads and the mussels that are not yet replenishing themselves. Much of the fjord is still waiting for pollution levels to fall. But in some places, the team's work is already helping life return.

How to find the middle of nowhere

Sometimes you just want to be left alone. But where would you go?

We scoured the map to find the places you are least likely to bump into other humans – the spots furthest from any road. We discovered that in most European countries, you're never more than 10 kilometres from the nearest road.

But at the heart of Iceland's Vatnajökull glacier lies Europe's most remote location, which would require a trek of at least 46 kilometres to reach. Draw a perfect circle around this point and you get an area of almost 7,000 square kilometres – more than four times the size of London – that is largely devoid of people.

Toon Vos

Last but not least

In her latest book, British novelist Deborah Levy explores everything she's learned from Gertrude Stein: an avant-garde American poet, queer icon, and art collector who made Paris her home in the early 20th century. “It's about Stein, but at the same time, it's not at all about Stein,” Levy said during a talk held in Brussels in late October.

Among a very diverse crowd of fans, I was there as an admirer of her Living Autobiography trilogy. I hadn't bought her new book yet, but by the end of her talk, I was convinced. Now that I've read it, I must say she's done a brilliant job of selling it.

While it can certainly be read as a biography of Stein, the book also blends fiction, art history, and a little memoir. It's about Stein, but mostly about friendship, identity, composition, and how to put yourself together – plot twist: Levy doesn't come up with a ready-made solution. It also explores what it means to be a female writer in the 21st century.

For the biggest Deborah Levy fans among our readers, she also hinted that her trilogy might soon become a quartet...

Marie-Flore Pirmez

Buy the book

“Plans trip to Vatnajökull glacier.”

Claire Brown

NEWSLETTER · 27 Nov 2026, 06:10

Macron: budget hero or villain?

Also, Phil Hogan takes a step towards Rome

VIEW IN BROWSER

By Eddy Wax

with Nicoletta Ionta

Supported by

Good morning. It’s Friday 27 November. You can reach us here.

In today’s Rapporteur AM:

Macron pitches himself as budget negotiator

Spain’s election campaign hits climax

Phil Hogan inches closer to UN gig

On the roundabout: The next EUCO could be a six-shirter

Supported by Martens Centre

The European Ideas Forum (EIF) is back!

Join us on December 8&9 at the DoubleTree by Hilton in Brussels, as we explore the key challenges facing Europe and the ideas shaping the EU’s response. Register here.

From the capital

Emmanuel Macron was the first leader to address journalists at the EU summit on Thursday – while other leaders were still upstairs negotiating.

Seizing the opportunity to set the agenda, he made a shameless pitch for himself as the EU’s de facto budget negotiator.

“I'm trying to bring everyone closer together,” he told reporters, making out that he was merely defending the common good and the European interest.

Talks floundered at the summit last night after four ‘frugal’ countries – Denmark, Austria, Sweden, and Belgium – theatrically refused to join side meetings with small numbers of other countries, chaired by António Costa.

The “spirit of compromise” that the Council president had called for at the start of the day was in short supply, one senior EU official commented.

Leaders agreed to meet again in December, but it was unclear whether the much discussed ‘blood on the walls’ summit many predicted was a necessary prelude to a deal had really happened.

The next summit could be the moment for Macron to fill a yawning leadership gap at Costa’s side, as co-negotiator. It’s a role he played alongside Angela Merkel during the last budget talks.

But Macron’s pressure tactics this time around have not won him many admirers. On Thursday he again demanded that leaders reach a deal by the end of the year, refusing to negotiate if talks drag into 2026x which riled up the others.

Macron is probably the least popular person in the room, one senior diplomat told us. Giorgia Meloni railed against his December deadline threat, and Friedrich Merz rebuffed his claim to be the main negotiator, telling reporters there are 27 bridge-builders, not just one.

“Can we please call Macron Monsieur Chantage from now on?” another EU diplomat said. (Chantage means blackmail).

France has refused to join either of the two camps of the budget talks so far, flirting with the ‘frugal’ camp, and the ‘Friends of Cohesion’– which he attended on behalf of Spain.

Macron has a lengthy list of priorities, from a digital services tax, to embedding a European preference in EU spending, to farm subsidies, and no rebates or cuts.

After all, Macron has nothing to lose since he won’t be running in next year’s presidential election. But observers note that something much greater is at stake: his legacy as a leader on the European stage, and the French public’s perception of Europe at large.

If Marine Le Pen, whom he accused of arrogance at that same summit, wins next year, France’s approach to EU politics will radically change – likely disengaging from Europe, and Ukraine.

But striking a deal on Macron’s terms could help a future centrist candidate show that France can lead in Europe, and deliver results.

Will he emerge at next month’s summit as the Manu of the moment, or the villain who demanded too much?

Timeline tussle

Costa is now preparing a new ‘nego box’ – or compromise text – for as soon as the week after next.

But there were signs that the discussion is losing momentum. The summit reopened an age-old debate about when an EU budget deal is really needed. Many leaders rebuked Emmanuel Macron’s push to wrap things up by the end of the year.

Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, the Netherlands’ Rob Jetten, and Luxembourg’s Luc Frieden all pushed back on the supposed need to rush to a deal next month, prioritising substance over speed. Ulf Kristersson, the Swedish PM, said it will “have to take as long as it takes.” Lithuania’s president, Gitanas Nausėda, has already said a deal can be done early next year.

But Emmanuel Macron was adamant that he would simply refuse to negotiate if there is no deal by the end of the year.

“Life also goes on after the elections in France, Poland, Italy, and so on,” said Frieden. “We want to finish in December, but Europe will not collapse if we finish in January or February.”

Rapporteur’s analysis: The reopening of the debate on whether and when a budget deal is needed suggests a deal is not as close as Costa & Co. might like to think.

Good news for Phil Hogan

Phil Hogan, Ireland's former European commissioner, has moved closer to winning the EU's nomination to run the UN's Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), several diplomats told Rapporteur.

Hogan won the backing of Germany, whose Chancellor Friedrich Merz hails from the same conservative European People's Party family as the Irishman. Europe has been unable to choose between three candidates – Hogan, Spain's Luis Planas, and Italy's Maurizio Martina – a division that risks weakening the EU's hand.

Germany's backing is a potentially seismic shift that moves Hogan clearly into position as the frontrunner in Brussels. Read my full story.

Last tango in Madrid

The candidates for Spain’s general election locked horns in a four-way televised debate on Thursday evening, aiming to mobilise the undecided voters just three days before ballots are cast on Sunday, my colleague Inés Fernández-Pontes reports.

After weeks of intense campaigning, Spain’s electoral race is reaching a climax, with the latest opinion polls pointing to a rightward shift.

Pedro Sánchez, who skipped a summit of EU leaders in Brussels to prepare for the debate, framed the race as a choice between progressive advances and right-wing “regression”. Read the full piece.

Here are three new stories from Rapporteur:

Why Europe's cold snap hasn't caused gas price spikes – yet

EU-Ukraine drone alliance poised for major expansion

Open-source platform adds to AI cyber threats

Advertisement

Schuman roundabout

CLEAR YOUR CALENDARS: The next EU budget summit could stretch to a week. Leaders could be in for a marathon December summit, with talks on the bloc’s next long-term budget potentially dragging on for up to a week, one diplomat said.

And capitals are already preparing for long talks. Two EU countries have booked four nights in Brussels hotels for the summit starting 17 December, according to another EU diplomat and an EU official. Leaders are due to arrive on Wednesday 16 December, first for a meeting with Narendra Modi, the Indian prime minister, before diving into budget negotiations that could outlast the four-day marathon of 2020.

The capitals

🇫🇷 PARIS

Jordan Bardella, president of the far-right National Rally, came under renewed fire on Thursday following revelations by Le Monde and Mediapart about anti-Semitic writing from 2013, which Mediapart first brought to light in September. Bardella reiterated his “formal denial” of the messages, saying they do not reflect his ideas – either in the past or present. He denounced the media for carrying out “witch hunts”. Le Monde wrote that the evidence gathered “leaves no doubt that he did indeed write these messages”.

– Clara Vassent

🇩🇰 COPENHAGEN

Denmark's central population register has suffered another cyberattack, exposing the personal data of 11,000 people, the country's digital affairs ministry announced. The breach follows an October incident affecting 8.8 million records from the same database, which prompted authorities to tighten security procedures. The perpetrator of the latest attack remains unidentified. The incident comes as cybersecurity concerns grow across Europe. In September, Denmark's civil security authorities raised the national cyberattack threat level to “high”.

– Clara Vassent

🇮🇹 ROME

Italy's controversial hunting reform reached the lower house on Thursday, five months after the Senate approved the legislation. The centre-right government's proposal would extend hunting seasons and give regional authorities greater discretion to disregard recommendations from ISPRA, Italy's national wildlife research institute. The European Commission warned in a letter last December that both measures risk violating the EU Birds Directive. The legislation has drawn criticism over its potential impact on wildlife protection and compliance with European environmental rules.

– Alessia Peretti

🇵🇱 WARSAW

Poland's Constitutional Tribunal disciplinary court suspended its president, Bogdan Święczkowski, from judicial duties for 12 months, deepening a dispute over the court's leadership. Judge Magdalena Bentkowska said the decision followed Święczkowski's refusal to allow five judges elected by parliament to take up their duties. The ruling extends an initial one-month suspension imposed on 30 October by Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, head of the Constitutional Tribunal. The disciplinary court considers the five judges legitimate members of the tribunal from the date of their election.

– Charles Szumski

🇸🇰 BRATISLAVA

Robert Fico’s governing coalition has come up with yet another amendment to the Criminal Code. After already aiding several of its politicians by shortening statutes of limitations and reducing sentences, it now wants to abolish the criminal offence of accepting an undue advantage altogether. The opposition says this would also benefit Fico and his interior minister. It is not yet clear when MPs will vote on the proposal.

– Natália Silenská

🇧🇬 SOFIA

Eight people, including five municipal councillors and three private company representatives, were detained in Bulgaria on suspicion of involvement in a scheme to defraud EU funds, the European Public Prosecutor's Office said on Wednesday. Projects linked to Haskovo municipality, dating back to 2021, may have cost more than €70 million in EU funds. The projects received funding from the European Regional Development Fund and the Recovery and Resilience Facility. The investigation remains ongoing.

– Konstantin Karadjov

🇭🇷 ZAGREB

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković on Thursday said that Zagreb would block Montenegro from closing Chapter 31 of its EU accession negotiations until a longstanding border dispute is resolved. Plenković ruled out any changes to the boundary on the Prevlaka peninsula. His warning contradicts comments on Tuesday by Montenegro's European Affairs Minister Maida Gorčević, who insisted Croatia was not obstructing accession talks. Podgorica hopes to close its eight remaining negotiating chapters in December, but Croatia's objections could complicate that timetable.

– Bronwyn Jones

-Markte: Der gefahrliche Staatskapitalismus des Donald Trump

SAP-Chef Christian Klein (Foto: picture alliance/dpa)

Guten Morgen, liebe Leserin, lieber Leser,SAP plant nach Informationen meines Kollegen Christof Kerkmann den Abbau von mehr als 10.000 Stellen, ein Insider spricht sogar von bis zu 15.000, bei derzeit 113.000 Beschaftigten. Final ist der Plan noch nicht: Beschluss und Ankündigung dürften erst Anfang 2027 folgen. Der Konzern kommentiert „Spekulationen“ nicht, teilt aber mit:

KI verandert unser Geschaftsumfeld rasant.

Was sich gestern übrigens, wenn auch anders als beabsichtigt, zeigte: Nach einem Bericht des „Spiegel“ ist SAP derzeit auch Opfer eines https://click.redaktion.handelsblatt.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNzMsInQiOjk5NzEsInMiOjd9AAcAAAAACibtYs1Y2PVTEOb7mY7oNo32crZ_nLVz9URRBUtXfLzJ1-qDS_ykbjf1hv41R-5_OmuYpJWlQ8HE8HvfDcg4LAQZfLkXaYUhp4unlQ womoglich KI-gestützten Hackerangriffs .

Hinter dem Jobplan steht ein klares Ziel: Bis 2028 sollen sich die Produktivitatseffekte auf mehr als zwei Milliarden Euro summieren. Der Gedanke folgt einer gewissen Logik: Wer seinen Kunden verspricht, dass KI ihre Ablaufe effizienter macht, muss das zuerst im eigenen Haus vorführen. Ausgerechnet die Vorreiter der Technologie stehen deshalb unter Beweispflicht – Microsoft, Oracle und Salesforce haben bereits Stellen gestrichen, das verstarkt die Erwartungen an SAP.

Damit wird der Dax-Konzern zum Anwendungsfall dafür, wie KI den Arbeitsmarkt verandert. Denn Sparpotenzial sieht das Management vor allem „nah am Programmcode“ – also genau dort, wo bislang klassische Software-Spezialisten arbeiten. Gleichzeitig stellt SAP massiv ein: KI-Entwickler, Forscher und sogenannte „Forward Deployed Engineers“, die Produkte bei Kunden einführen. Es droht also eher andere als weniger Arbeit.

Daran wird man übrigens demnachst auch zukunftsfahige von weniger zukunftsfahigen Unternehmen auseinanderhalten konnen: Bei Ersteren fallen Stellen weg, dafür entstehen neue. Bei Letzteren, wir schauen unauffallig nach Wolfsburg oder Stuttgart, fallen einfach Stellen weg. Und so bleibt zunachst offen, ob SAP durch den Jobabbau am Ende wirklich kleiner wird. Nach früheren Restrukturierungen arbeiteten hinterher auch mal mehr Menschen für den Konzern als vorher. Gut moglich also, dass auch dieses Programm vor allem eines verandert: wer auf der Gehaltsliste steht – nicht, wie viele.

Markte: Der gefahrliche Staatskapitalismus des Donald Trump

Der Wahnsinn der Gegenwart zeigt sich seit zwei Wochen an den Aktienmarkten: Erst ging es steil bergab, dann – Jensen Huang war gerade als Nvidia-Chef zurückgekehrt – ebenso steil bergauf und wieder bergab. Was die Kurse nicht abbilden, bringt Okonom Mohamed El-Erian im Gesprach mit meinen Kollegen Astrid Dorner und Jens Münchrath auf den Punkt: https://click.redaktion.handelsblatt.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNzMsInQiOjk5NzEsInMiOjd9AAcAAAAACibtYs1dJ4HdVZQaBEGS27dSnRoUYz_aHCw5D9Q9A5xmhSAGRCOJZTHIpMy6dhXcWICqefcH_yUPuzHXNI0Ewsn3AQBhIX480cOvsw „Es ist kein Kapitalismus mehr, so wie wir ihn kannten.“

US-Prasident Donald Trump versucht, einen prasidial gelenkten Staatskapitalismus durchzusetzen, wie die an allen Instanzen vorbei durchgezogene Resozialisierung von Huang zeigte. Für die US-Wirtschaft geht es damit ans Eingemachte. Denn bislang galt: Es gewinnt das beste Produkt, nicht der beste Freund der Machtigen.

Wie verwundbar das Silicon Valley dadurch geworden ist, beschreiben die Autoren unserer Titelgeschichte: „Um seine sündhaft teure KI-Wette zu stemmen, hat das Silicon Valley auf einen Ikarus in Lederjacke und einen korrupten Prasidenten gewettet. Nun werden die Einsatze fallig.“ Unser Fazit: Früher schafften die Tech-Bros Innovationen, heute Probleme.

EZB-Chef: Es ist – schon wieder eine Eule

Der Spanier Pablo Hernández de Cos, bisher Chef der Bank für internationalen Zahlungsausgleich (BIZ), soll neuer Prasident der Europaischen Zentralbank werden. Weil sich Deutschland nach einem Deal zwischen Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz und Frankreichs Staatsprasident Emmanuel Macron bereits den machtigen Posten des EZB-Chefvolkswirts für Markus Brunnermeier gesichert hat, kommt die Personalie nicht überraschend. Sie entspricht dem typischen europaischen Ausgleichsprinzip, wonach ein „deutscher Falke“ auf einem machtigen Posten durch eine „südeuropaische Taube“ auf einem anderen kompensiert werden muss. Nur entspricht es auch der Realitat?

Schon die Einsortierung Brunnermeiers als lupenreiner Falke halt einer genaueren Uberprüfung nicht stand. Auch Hernández de Cos entzieht sich der klassischen Rubrizierung. Als er vor einiger Zeit gefragt wurde, wo er sich selbst sieht, zitierte er die Selbsteinschatzung der scheidenden EZB-Chefin Christine Lagarde: Die hatte sich zum Amtsantritt als „Eule“ bezeichnet, ein kleiner Spaß gegen die Traditionswachter.

Viel Zeit für Ausflüge ins Tierreich wird dem neuen EZB-Chef und seiner Führungsspitze ohnehin nicht bleiben. Die Inflation liegt bei rund vier Prozent, doch jede weitere Zinserhohung wird für hoch verschuldete Euro-Lander heikler. Wer sich da in Taube-Falke-Eule-Stellungsspielen verkampft, übersieht womoglich die Ankunft eines weiteren Federviehs: des Pleitegeiers.

Commerzbank: Der geordnete Ubergang

Seit gestern hat Unicredit alle Genehmigungen für die Ubernahme der Commerzbank beisammen. Und Andrea Orcel macht Tempo: Der Unicredit-Chef will den Umbau der Frankfurter Bank personlich als Aufsichtsratschef steuern, neun von zehn Kapitalvertretern im Kontrollgremium will er auf einer außerordentlichen Hauptversammlung austauschen. Vom Aufsichtsrat verlangt er zudem Aufhebungsvertrage mit mehreren Vorstanden. Bisher ist aber unklar, wer genau gehen soll – außer bei einer: Bettina Orlopp.

Die Commerzbank-Chefin hat lange für die Eigenstandigkeit ihres Hauses gekampft. Hinwerfen will sie trotzdem nicht:

Uns als Vorstand ist es ein wichtiges Anliegen, einen geordneten Ubergang sicherzustellen.

Das ist Haltung – und die eigentliche Pointe dieser Ubernahmeschlacht: Am Ende organisiert ausgerechnet die Managerin, die die Ubernahme verhindern wollte, den reibungslosen Einzug des Kaufers.

IG Metall: Und sie einigen sich doch

Wer zu 24-Stunden-Streiks aufruft, kann auch 24 Stunden verhandeln. Nach diesem Motto haben IG Metall und Arbeitgeber eine Losung im Tarifstreit gesucht – und auch gestern gefunden. Die 3,7 Millionen Beschaftigten der Metall- und Elektroindustrie bekommen im Marz eine Einmalzahlung von 150 bis 450 Euro, ab Mai 2027 zwei Prozent mehr, ab April 2028 weitere 2,3 Prozent – bei 25 Monaten Laufzeit. Gestartet war die IG Metall mit fünf Prozent für zwolf Monate.

Die Unternehmen bekommen dafür Luft: Wer weniger als 2,3 Prozent Nettoumsatzrendite erzielt, darf weiter Tarifbestandteile verschieben oder streichen, ohne vorher zu verhandeln. Neu ist ein Tarifvertrag, mit dem Betriebe Entgelte senken oder Arbeitszeit ohne Lohnausgleich verlangern konnen – wenn sie im Gegenzug investieren oder Standorte sichern. Notig ist das: Die Produktion liegt 15 Prozent unter dem Niveau von 2018, jeden Monat fallen rund 10.000 Jobs weg.

Zum Schluss schauen wir nach Kopenhagen, wo mein Kollege Thorsten Firlus einen Recherchetermin hatte, um den ich ihn beneide: Er besuchte Küche und Koch des „Alchemist“, des teuersten Restaurants Europas. Ein Laden, in dem stets alle Platze wenige Minuten nach der Freigabe reserviert sind. Die Warteliste enthalt pro zwei Monate rund 60.000 Namen. Und dennoch macht Küchenchef Rasmus Munk jetzt erstmal zu. Er will sich und seinen Leuten mehr Zeit gonnen, sich weiterzuentwickeln, zu reflektieren. Und Munk? Geht endlich selbst essen, sagt er. Der Mann mit der wohl langsten Warteliste Europas bekommt also auch mal einen Tisch.

... Milliarden Euro verdienten die 40 DAX-Konzerne in den ersten neun Monaten des Jahres nach Abzug aller Kosten. Damit übertrafen sie den Vorjahreswert um 8,6 Prozent. https://click.redaktion.handelsblatt.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNzMsInQiOjk5NzEsInMiOjd9AAcAAAAACibtYs2TMB6hhuYpunTGGJo32L2U90_rpWALHmymh3UVQBKAsmlZiL5Ren3KhcD96mQrE_6f6nOPTqvTfW8ewOP-BntXYci6oEVukw Berechnungen des Handelsblatt Research Institute zeigen, dass sich der bereits im ersten Halbjahr sichtbare Gewinntrend auch im dritten Quartal fortsetzte. Elf Konzerne steigerten ihren Nettogewinn um mehr als 30 Prozent. Dazu zahlen die Industrieunternehmen Airbus, BASF, Daimler Truck und Siemens Energy, der Pharmakonzern Bayer sowie die Finanzwerte Commerzbank und Deutsche Borse.

Dear friends,

I look forward to seeing many of you at AI Dev in New York City on Monday Nov 30th!

It is Thanksgiving here in the U.S., and I am reflecting on how grateful I am to be part of the AI community and for the incredible opportunities that lie ahead of us. Changes in AI are letting us do work at a pace and quality that was almost unimaginable a year ago. At the same time, this puts pressure on everyone to learn new skills. Despite AI’s amazing ability to solve verifiable tasks — like solve math problems such as the Riemann hypothesis — its far weaker performance on unverifiable tasks that require judgement means much work remains for people to do.

I am fortunate to have many friends across Silicon Valley and beyond, whom I meet and sometimes collaborate with and who help keep me sharp at the cutting edge of AI. I know that not everyone has similar opportunities, which is why I treasure in-person events like AI Dev.

AI Dev New York 2026 will focus on the AI Engineering Skills Map, which shows the most valuable skills for you to know to become skilled in AI Engineering. We have mapped every skill on the map — like building agentic systems, making systems secure and reliable, and coding agent foundations — to particular AI Dev sessions. I aim for everyone who attends to come away with meaningful new skills in AI Engineering, and also to come away with new friends so our community becomes stronger!

The AI world can feel crazy some days, with rapid changes coming every week. I’m grateful for the many people in my life — professional and personal — who help me to experience life at a slower, more human pace. I hope you all have a chance to slow down and enjoy the company of friends and family over the coming holidays.

Perhaps I’ll see you next week at AI Dev. Until then, Happy Thanksgiving!

With gratitude,

Andrew

News

Carbon, Hydrogen, Neon, Oh My!

Google introduced two faster, less expensive Gemini 4 models and a way for its coding agent to hand work back and forth between models mid-task.

What's new: On November 12, Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a model built to carry out coding and other agentic tasks quickly and at lower cost than Gemini 4 Carbon. On November 18, the company added Gemini 4 Neon, a model that rivals Carbon’s performance at an intermediate speed and cost. In addition, Antigravity, Google’s counterpart to OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code, gained Orchestrator, an option that allows larger models like Carbon or Neon to plan a task and have smaller models like Hydrogen carry it out.

Input/output: Text, images, audio, and video in, text out (up to 1 million tokens of input and output combined; up to 64,000 output token by default

Speed: Hydrogen, 173 tokens per second at its highest setting; Neon, 99 tokens per second, both according to Artificial Analysis

Architecture: Adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon

Price: Hydrogen $1.50/$7.50 per million input/output tokens via API; Neon $3.00/$15.00 per million input/tokens

Weights/license: Proprietary

Undisclosed: Parameter count, architecture details, how Google adapted Hydrogen or Neon from Carbon, training data and methods

How it works: Orchestrator divides each task between a planner and an executor instead of running one model for everything, according to Antigravity’s documentation. Unlike setups that split a task between different agents, Orchestrator keeps a single agent within a single context window (conversation) and switches the model behind it.

First, the planner (either Carbon, Neon, or Argon) studies the code without changing anything. Then it writes a plan that spells out what the actor model should do.

Hydrogen carries out the plan: It changes the code, builds and tests it, and confirms that the results match what the plan called for.

Hydrogen hands control back to the planner when it runs into trouble, such as a check that fails twice or an interface that behaves differently than expected. The planner rewrites the plan according to Hydrogen's feedback, then passes the work back.

Performance: Hydrogen trades some of Carbon’s capability for speed and lower cost, according to independent tests. Using Carbon as a planning model and Hydrogen as an actor inside Orchestrator nearly matches using Carbon alone, according to Google. Neon, meanwhile, outperforms Carbon on overall intelligence while costing less per task.

Hydrogen set to high reasoning scored 51 on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, roughly matching Gemini 4 Argon (50). Set to xhigh, Hydrogen scored 54, took 14.9 minutes, and cost $3.16 per task. Neon at xhigh scored 61, costing $6.44 per task and taking 25.8 minutes per task. Carbon set to high scored 60, took 32 minutes, and cost $5.48 per task at its introductory price.

Google says that on Terminal-Bench, which tests an agent’s ability to complete tasks in a computer terminal, using Carbon and Hydrogen together in Orchestrator came close to Carbon’s success rate while finishing 19 percent faster and consuming 24 percent less of its token quota on average.

Hydrogen’s lower price doesn’t always mean fewer tokens. Set to extra-high, Hydrogen generated 304 million output tokens over the Intelligence Index’s tests, compared with Carbon’s 205 million.

Behind the news: Google made Gemini 4 Carbon widely available on November 10, following Argon in September. The power and cost of Gemini’s models roughly correspond with the weight of their element names: Hydrogen is light and fast, while Carbon is relatively heavier and more substantial. But the elementally heavier Neon is faster than Carbon, and Argon, now the least capable of Gemini’s “element” models, is heaviest of all.

Why it matters: Pairing a cheaper model with a costlier one isn’t new. Anthropic’s Claude Code offers a related “advisor” option, in which a cheaper model does the work and consults a stronger one at key moments, such as before committing to a plan or when it gets stuck. OpenAI’s Codex lets developers assign different models to subagents, but it delegates work to them only when instructed. Sakana’s Fugu takes this logic one step further, using a dedicated orchestrator model that can call models from Google, OpenAI, or Anthropic at each step. All these efforts show that the best model for a coding task may turn out to be two or more models working together.

We’re thinking: Google has made three very capable new models available within the last month. We can all be thankful for this rapid pace of progress.

llama.cpp Makes It Official

llama.cpp, an open source software package that helps users run AI language models locally, finally reached version 1.0 after more than three years in development. The milestone signals that its developers consider it mature and stable enough for a major release.

What’s new: The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face released version 1.0.0 of llama.cpp and of ggml, the library that performs its underlying math. The release shows that llama.cpp is still widely used and under active development, and that local AI is arguably more popular than ever. The new package adds support for several new models, including Kimi-K3.1 Pro, a text-to-speech feature for its built-in server, and a redesigned chat interface.

How it works: Georgi Gerganov started llama.cpp in March 2023, about a week after Meta’s first LLaMA language model leaked online. Gerganov wrote it as a plain C/C++ program, compiled to run directly on a computer’s processor. Meta’s own code for running LLaMA required Python, the PyTorch framework, CUDA, and an Nvidia graphics chip. Gerganov’s version had no dependencies and could run on a MacBook or any other machine, regardless of whether it had a specific GPU. Llama.cpp has been in use ever since, powering apps like Ollama and LM Studio that likewise help run local AI models on ordinary machines.

While it’s perhaps best known for running AI models on laptops, llama.cpp can perform inference on hardware that ranges from servers to edge machines. The project supports “more than 150 architecture variants,” the team says.

llama.cpp loads models stored in GGUF, a file format designed to load quickly. Hugging Face hosts thousands of models compatible with llama.cpp.

The software relies heavily on quantization, which shrinks a model by storing its weights (the numbers that encode what it learned) at lower precision, for instance as 4-bit instead of 32-bit numbers. Quantized models require less memory and often run faster, sometimes at a cost in accuracy.

The ggml library interacts with different kinds of hardware through separate backends, modules written for specific chips or programming standards. These include CUDA for Nvidia GPUs, Metal for Apple chips, and the cross-vendor Vulkan standard, as well as backends for ordinary CPUs.

A bundled server accepts requests in formats modeled on OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s APIs, so many apps written for cloud models can use a local model instead. The project makes “no strong claims of compatibility” with OpenAI’s specification but says the server “suffices to support many apps.”

Behind the news: llama.cpp’s 1.0 release caps a period of steady growth for the project.

GitHub’s annual Octoverse report ranked llama.cpp fifth among independent open-source projects for growth in contributors this year, and third in overall engagement.

Development is constant. The project published 50 nightly builds over November 15 and 16 alone, and version 1.0 arrived nine days after version 0.9.0.

Hugging Face, which the ggml team joined in February 2026, provides the project with “long-term sustainable resources,” the team said at the time, and Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM, and Intel supply hardware for self-hosted test runners, according to the v1.0.0 announcement.

Why it matters: llama.cpp turned running language models from a data-center job into something a laptop can do. That lets people and organizations keep their data on their own machines, consult AI without an Internet connection, and avoid paying a cloud provider for every token. Because so many tools now build on llama.cpp, the project’s continued health matters to everyone who uses them, not just to its own developers.

We’re thinking: Kudos to llama.cpp’s founding team and its growing community of developers! Anyone who works on open source and open models can draw inspiration from their achievements.

One successful run does not mean your agent is reliable. Learn to read your agent’s traces to find recurring failures, build code evaluators and LLM judges you can trust, and use evals to check that each change makes your agent better. Enroll now

How the “Token Tax” Hurts Non-English Users

Using AI models costs non-Western speakers in emerging markets far more than they do for English speakers. A recent study quantifies the difference across more than 200 languages.

What’s new: All language models break words into tokens. But not every language is tokenized equally well. Low-resource languages are not well-served by popular existing tokenizers. According to a study published by the Coalition for Language Equity in AI Research (CLEAR), token counts (and therefore cost) for identical content can be up to 17 times higher for the worst-served languages than for the most efficiently tokenized ones.

How it works: Tokenizers turn text into tokens based on how frequently sequences of characters appear in an LLM’s training data. That means that the more often a language’s words appear in a data set, the more efficiently that language can be turned into meaningful blocks. Meanwhile, languages with less representation are split into much smaller segments, leading to significantly higher token counts per word or phrase. This leads to a correspondingly higher cost for the exact same content.

CLEAR showed that in GPT-5, the same sentence in English (“People should benefit from AI, regardless of the language they speak”), Malayalam (“ആളുകൾ ഏത് ഭാഷ സംസാരിക്കുന്നവരായാലും, AI-യിൽ നിന്ന് പ്രയോജനം നേടണം”), and the East African language Amharic (“ሰዎች የሚናገሩት ቋንቋ ምንም ይሁን ምን ከ AI ተጠቃሚ መሆን አለባቸው።”) costs 13 tokens, 26 tokens, and 78 tokens, respectively, even though the difference in character counts is negligible.

CLEAR tallied the maximum/minimum token count ratio for tokenizers across the FLORES-200 languages (204 low-resource language and script pairs) and, on either end of the scale, gave the tokenizers an A for a ratio of three times or less and an F for a ratio exceeding 12 times. Many of what were then the most advanced, general-purpose AI models’ tokenizers — GPT-5 and Llama 3.3 among them — got an F, while Google’s Gemini/Gemma family earned the study’s best grade, a B.

Behind the news: This isn’t the first time that a light has been shone on token bias. CLEAR cites two 2023 studies that were among the first to examine the issue.

In “Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages,” presented at NeurIPS in 2023, Petrov et al. argued that tokenization differences didn’t just cost more (15 times in their study), but also slowed down AI inference for some global users.

In “Do All Languages Cost the Same,” Ahia et al. analyzed OpenAI’s popular language model API across 22 typologically diverse languages and found that speakers of many of them, particularly languages with scripts underrepresented in training data, were overcharged for the same content while also getting poorer results.

A 2024 study on GPT-4o found that its tokenizer contained many overly long Chinese tokens, a large share of them drawn from spam, gambling, and adult-content web text. GPT-4o handled these tokens worse than GPT-4 did, which the authors tie to how the tokenizer treats long, statistically frequent vocabulary items from noisy training data.

While some tokenizers have improved, newer models within a family can actually perform worse than their predecessors. In the CLEAR study, Alibaba’s Qwen 3.6 had a max/min token count ratio of 13.1 times, while the older Qwen 3 had one of 10.5 times.

Why it matters: Startups and users in emerging markets are already at a disadvantage when it comes to getting the reliable connectivity and/or computing power required to use most LLMs. Adding a tax for local languages restricts the worldwide market for AI and pushes more queries to Roman scripts or other global languages like Mandarin Chinese. This reduces our planetary linguistic diversity to something closer to a monoculture.

We’re thinking: As linguistic units, tokens capture meaning better than whole words or individual characters, but where one token stops and the next begins is still quite arbitrary. We need continued textual scholarship and ethnographic work to properly capture nuances in meaning within these languages and their scripts. Better tokenization should be part of that effort too. This will ensure better translation and generation as well as more equitable pricing.

Communicating Agents’ Thoughts

When one AI agent sends a text message to another, the tokens it sends contain less information than the hidden states of the agent’s LLM. Researchers enabled agents based on the same LLM to transmit hidden states without further training.

What’s new: Yanwen Peng and colleagues at the University of Sheffield developed StateBridge, a method that enables agents that are based on the same LLM to communicate with one another through hidden states without further training. The code is freely available for both commercial and noncommercial uses under the Apache 2.0 license.

Key insight: Each token a sender agent writes has two vectors: (i) the hidden state computed by the final layer of the sender agent's model prior to generating the token, which holds information such as the agent's confidence in the token and traces of alternatives it did not choose, and (ii) the resulting token embedding. Sending the token embedding alone loses information in the hidden state. Sending the hidden state keeps that information, but the receiver cannot read it: The two vectors point in different directions and differ greatly in magnitude, and the receiver was pretrained to take token embeddings as its input. So the hidden states have to be moved toward the receiver’s input space. This is the key to communicating the sender agent’s thoughts directly.

How it works: The researchers built agents based on three Qwen3 models (4, 8, and 32 billion parameters) and OLMo3-7B-Think. To produce inter-agent communications, they used four agents in sequence: planner, critic, refiner, judge (roles defined by LatentMAS, an earlier method that feeds the sender agent’s key-value cache into every layer of the receiver agent’s model). Given a prompt, the planner outlines a response, the critic checks the plan, the refiner revises the plan, and the judge uses the revised plan to produce final output. At each handoff, the StateBridge method converts the sender’s hidden states into vectors the receiver takes as input in place of the sender’s generated tokens.

The authors paired the sender’s hidden states with their token embeddings. The sender generated its message, such as the planner’s plan, as text, one token at a time. The authors kept the hidden states of the message’s last 64 tokens, since later hidden states reflect more of the preceding text.

They rotated the hidden states toward their token embeddings. They normalized both sets of vectors, the 64 hidden states, and their 64 token embeddings, so both had a mean of zero and equal variance. Then the authors found the single rotation that brought the hidden states, on average, as close as possible to their own token embeddings without modifying the distances and angles between the hidden states. Last, they scaled the rotated hidden states to the token embeddings’ original mean and variance.

After the rotation, they gave every hidden state the same magnitude. Matching the token embeddings’ mean and variance adjusted the hidden states as a set, not one by one, so individual hidden states could still be larger than token embeddings. In this way, they scaled each hidden state to the average magnitude of all the token embeddings in the model’s vocabulary.

They modified each hidden state to be more similar to its closest token embedding. For each hidden state, they searched the vocabulary for the token embedding that pointed in the direction most similar to that hidden state’s. (It didn’t necessarily correspond to the token the sender wrote.) They replaced each hidden state with a weighted average: 70 percent the hidden state and 30 percent its closest token embedding. This weighted average moved each hidden state to be more similar to the kinds of inputs the receiver saw during pretraining.

They prepended the resulting 64 hidden states to the token embeddings of the receiver’s prompt. The receiver then became the sender and generated the next message. (The judge‘s message was the final response).

Results: The authors tested StateBridge with the Qwen3 models and OLMo3-7B-Think. The tests included answering questions (MedQA), coding (HumanEval+), and math (GSM8K) plus, for the two larger Qwen3 models, further math and science benchmarks (such as GPQA-Diamond). With every model tested, their method achieved higher average results than three alternatives (a single agent working alone, the same four agents handing off text, and LatentMAS). It outperformed the best of them by 2.4 to 2.9 percentage points.

StateBridge achieved its largest margin over the strongest alternative on GPQA-Diamond’s graduate-level science questions. With Qwen3-8B, agents using StateBridge solved 52.5 percent of the questions, compared with 45.5 percent using LatentMAS and 39.9 percent using a single agent.

With OLMo3-7B-Think, agents using StateBridge solved an average of 76.7 percent of problems across benchmarks while the strongest alternative, four agents exchanging text, achieved 73.9 percent.

LatentMAS solved 55.1 percent, below a single agent (71.8 percent).

Why it matters: Compared to text communication, StateBridge raised the average performance of multi-agent systems for every model tested. And the barrier to experimentation is low, since you can jump straight in without needing to collect training data or train a model.

We’re thinking: StateBridge passes along only the hidden states for the last 64 tokens of each message, however long the message. Yet agents that used StateBridge achieved higher average scores than agents that handed off the full text. If 64 converted hidden states can stand in for a whole message, similar conversions might let agents pass other long inputs, such as retrieved documents or tool outputs, as a small number of vectors.

Snapshot of the day

November 26, 2026

Anirudh S.K., Kalrav Joshi

India on Thursday commemorated 77 years since its Constitution was adopted. Fittingly, the events of the day produced a few signs that these days the ideals and articles of this text are being honoured more in the breach than the observance.

One of these was the Modi government’s cryptic announcement, made an unprecedented 105 days after the monsoon session of parliament was adjourned but not prorogued, that it is set to hold a sitting starting Monday to “to transact essential Government Business”. What exactly this business is minister Kiren Rijiju elected not to say, notwithstanding parliament’s status as the ‘temple of democracy’, but the likely agenda is that his government will have a second whack at moving its delimitation package.

Quite a bit has changed from the time it made its first, abortive attempt to accomplish this in April: since then the ruling alliance has managed to secure defections from the Trinamool Congress – via an unrecognised shell party – the Shiv Sena (UBT) and the Aam Aadmi Party; indeed speculation is rife that the NDA has now mustered the magic two-thirds number it needs to get its delimitation agenda through the Lok Sabha and amend the Constitution. Meanwhile, the 22-member-strong Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam stands alienated from the INDIA bloc, and in another jolt to the opposition, Supriya Sule of the Nationalist Congress Party’s Sharad Pawar faction signalled that her outfit’s stance on the delimitation agenda is flexible. “First let the Bill come. Let the entire Bill come into our hands … if the Bill is good for the nation, we might support it,” she told reporters.

No draft of an amended delimitation Bill has been released but reports indicate that it will, unlike last time, contain a written provision for increasing the number of Lok Sabha seats by 50% across all states and Union territories. Even if every state retains its proportion of seats, concerns remain over what it will take to smoothly run an 850-seat House and how the existing scheme of seats will be shaken up (what happened in Assam and Jammu and Kashmir is not encouraging; scroll down to Opeds for more). The Lok Sabha is to convene on Monday and the Rajya Sabha on Wednesday; the sitting is to last all the way through… Thursday.

A couple other, more familiar ones also unfolded in Delhi. Protesters seeking chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over the troubled rollout of the special intensive revision were once again met with barricades and prohibitory orders. Over 200 people turned up anyway at Mandir Marg – almost exactly two months after the Indian Express‘s exposé precipitated public anger against the SIR – from where they could not proceed to the now-denotified protest site of Jantar Mantar Road. So they stayed put. (Just like CEC Kumar has, wherever he is. Amid his weekslong public absence the official seems to have been spotted in Bhopal this week; more on that in Reportedly.)

At the other end of Lutyens’ Delhi, in the high court, it was revealed that on top of the passport authorities sending an eleventh-hour notice to Cockroach Janta Party leader Saurav Das to prevent him from addressing students in Britain, ...

Executive Briefing

Bank of Korea raises rates as chip boom drives sharp upgrade to growth outlook

John Lee

The Bank of Korea (BOK) raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 3.25% on Thursday in a 5-2 decision, while raising its economic growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 from 3.3% and 2.9% to 3.9% and 4.1%, respectively. Its 2027 projection exceeds the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) forecast of 3.3% and the Korea Development Institute’s (KDI) estimate of 3.9%.

The central bank maintained its 2026 inflation forecast at 2.7% and raised its 2027 projection from 2.3% to 2.4%, with core inflation expected to reach 2.6% in both years. The Monetary Policy Board signaled further rate increases, with its six-month conditional interest rate projections ranging from 3.25% to 3.75% and a median of 3.5%.

Russia plays dangerous airspace game

Korea Times

"South Korea has good reason to remain vigilant amid Russia’s increasingly frequent KADIZ incursions. After beginning its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russia has revived its Cold War-era friendship with North Korea. In December 2024, the two countries signed the Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, elevating their relationship to an alliance. Article 4 of the treaty stipulates mutual defense, committing both sides to provide immediate military and other assistance through all available means if either comes under armed attack."

26 November, 2026

Alex Binley

Hello. Storms are bringing severe weather to both US coasts - we've got more on the impact. A year on from a fire that ripped through a Hong Kong apartment complex, killing 168, we meet the families waiting for justice. And finally, find out exactly what a "turkey bomber" is.

TOP OF THE AGENDA

Major US storms disrupt flights and leave hundreds of thousands without power

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNzIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB94TrbJVcxNYPtzUFXAyopjW5ZnlQ89mDHrGk3eJ9pRStJgvhCuVMB45ZrBWUwQC6EXO_KCbCm4YyrPQ7y_dyW6ZNv1dBipICHKxSfe60w Strong winds, heavy rain and flooding are hitting large parts of the US. Credit: Reuters

Thousands of Americans' Thanksgiving plans are in disarray as storms batter the US. More than 400 flights have been cancelled so far and another 1,700 have been delayed during what was expected to be one of the US's busiest travel periods of the year. Wet and windy weather has left almost 800,000 people without power predominantly across Virginia, Missouri and Maryland, and a state of emergency has been declared in New Jersey. Meanwhile on the west coast, a "king tide" could see water levels along California's coastline reach over 8ft (2.4 metres), breaking records set just this week. AT THE SCENE

Hong Kong

A renovation was meant to improve these Hong Kong homes - it ended in a blaze that killed 168

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNzIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB94TrbJsc1kGJkXL6glYGfl8goAS9ADjbX73wB_utrUhfxH0wZrbkyRvOJrHZZKeDx3Q1SOZN46ktRSIeBHKGIbEqB-g5CWkAUUeGJ-Edg Christy's husband was home alone when the fire broke out.

A year after one of Hong Kong's deadliest fires, the families left behind are still waiting for justice. A final report into the blaze at Wang Fuk Court that killed 168 people said the tragedy that took place during renovations was entirely preventable and happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption.

Grace Tsoi, BBC World Service, Phoebe Kong, BBC Chinese, and Yvette Tan, senior journalist

Christy's husband died in the stairwell from smoke inhalation. She says she's planning to file a lawsuit against those responsible for the fire, but acknowledges that even if she wins, she "can't [get] my husband's life back". "I share things that happen... as if he still existed," she says. "I often write to him, 'I miss you so much. Are you doing well on the other side?'"

It's a similar story for Mrs Lau, who says she can't go anywhere without seeing her husband who died in their flat. "Every day, something reminds me of him," she says. "I find it very hard to accept that my husband is gone, my home is gone, and so many of my neighbours are gone."

Sofia Lotto Persio

Hello. European authorities investigating migrant smugglers suspect a German man of supplying them with equipment - read our investigation. We speak to the US pastor who wants to see women's right to vote overturned. And finally, watch a remarkable one-handed catch.

TOP OF THE AGENDA

German boat dealer suspected of supplying smuggling gangs

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNzIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB9KWVR6b4pY6FTiHfO-Sb3cRJlHOfXfSuQ8WHC0T73unADS66KtSYlF5qycD3JS8Y0opa8-CisRgP7-__y3559S6eIfN4d1CuoNgyeeX A press photo from 2021 - migrants in a boat from Marvin Reuter's firm (logo circled). Credit: Getty Images

A logo can sometimes be spotted on the small boats used by migrants attempting to cross the English Channel: MaRe Boote, a German company. Its managing director, Marvin Reuter, is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers. Nearly a third of crossings in early 2026 allegedly involved boats or engines from his firm, according to files seen by us. It is suspected that his equipment was linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died. Reuter is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges. He can't be formally charged until then, and is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Read our investigation https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNzIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB9KWVR6cCSfrbMifVQ7cVgk8FPzX4If-7SEKNn38i7swOEqgy8EzAyLbewmxYyqEXA36mptEFtQax5RDhTYwsgOWKdGaShtEKA2HPn9J

BEYOND THE HEADLINES

The controversial US pastor Pete Hegseth calls his mentor

Wilson's Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches, has around 150 churches in the US.

A self-described Christian nationalist, Pastor Doug Wilson believes the US should be a theocracy, with gay sex criminalised, abortion outlawed, and people of other faiths unable to hold public office. But it's his views on repealing women's right to vote that have attracted the most headlines. Due to his association with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, his beliefs have been thrust under the spotlight. Wilson's views may represent a fringe perspective amongst Christians in the US, but they have been gaining support.
