NEWSLETTER · 26 Nov 2026, 18:01

Costa plays EU budget therapist

Also, in tonight’s edition: Ukraine movements, US defence review and CAP changes

VIEW IN BROWSER

By Victoria Becker

António Costa’s two-day special summit is well underway and could be over in just one.

In the theatre of EU budget negotiations, the meeting before the deal is often designed to fail.

Diplomats had predicted a proverbial bloodbath, setting the stage for a later breakthrough. But with little sense of urgency among national capitals, the mood so far is more lukewarm puddle than bloodbath.

Costa, the European Council president and MFF’s master puppeteer, is pulling leaders into a series of mix-and-match huddles, bringing together smaller groups spanning the political, financial and geographical divides.

Diplomats have dubbed them “group therapy sessions” – an attempt to get leaders who would not normally speak to one another around the same table discussing what they might have in common as well what sets them apart.

Their meetings will end when the clock strikes midnight (at least according to the plan).

Only then will Costa decide whether the 26 – Spain’s Pedro Sánchez is represented by Emmanuel Macron, the French president, with Spain heading into early elections on Sunday – will be called back for a second round on Friday.

But expectations of a Black Friday budget special are low.

Follow our live blog for more.

Round-up

AGRI COPE: The European Commission is planning targeted changes to the Common Agricultural Policy legislation to allow member states to provide cash flow for farmers coping with fuel and energy prices, according to a draft regulation obtained by Rapporteur.

UKRAINE SWAY: The German push to link the next EU budget to future support for Kyiv has divided capitals, with Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia and Bulgaria initially rejecting the plan. However, indications suggest Merz’s threat to veto the budget deal if the two files are not linked could succeed, and that some holdout countries have been swayed.

EXCLUSIVE: The US force posture review announcement, initially tabled for December, has been delayed until next year, NATO diplomats confirmed to Rapporteur on Thursday. The review was meant to last six months with the aim of scaling back Washington’s military presence in Europe and what it could provide NATO allies in times of crisis.

NEWSLETTER · 26 Nov 2026, 16:42

Brussels’ lobbying world still favors Western Europe

A weekly newsletter on campaigning, lobbying and political influence in the EU. By MARI ECCLES Hello and welcome to EU Influence! I'm Mari Eccles. On

A weekly newsletter on campaigning, lobbying and political influence in the EU.

By MARI ECCLES

Tips, tales, traumas to influence@politico.eu | View in your browser

Hello and welcome to EU Influence! I’m Mari Eccles. On the agenda this week:

The EU’s lobbying bubble has a central eastern blind spot.

NGOs hit back after Parliament report calls for funding cuts.

How Big Oil outmaneuvered Brussels.

ON THE RECORD

“We don’t do that much here, at the end of the day,” long-time consultant Aaron McLoughlin on life in the Brussels bubble (and why we should go back to our home countries more often).

UNEQUAL UNION

BLOC-ED OUT?: Consultants from Central and Eastern European countries are hugely under-represented in Brussels — and those that do work here get worse access to the EU institutions than their counterparts from Western Europe, according to new research shared exclusively with Influence.

Credit: ACCESS4ALL project at Maastricht University

Institutional breakdown: In the Council, researchers found that 72% of meeting requests from consultants based in older member states were successful, compared with 37% from CEE consultants. Things are a little better for CEE public affairs professionals wanting to speak to policymakers in the European Commission and European Parliament, although there was still a difference in success rate (79% versus 70% in the Parliament, 78% against 72% in the Commission).

In numbers: CEE countries account for a fifth of the EU population, but only one in 10 public affairs professionals in Brussels come from those countries, according to the research, conducted by academics at Maastricht University.

What’s behind it?: As part of the research, the academics asked the professionals — including people working for consultancies, NGOs and industry — to rate their own skills, to see if that played into the disparity in meeting request rate. It didn’t. Professionals rated themselves equally, no matter their nationality. “Our findings suggest that differences in professional skills cannot explain why some lobbyists find it harder to get a meeting,” said Iskander De Bruycker, who led the project, called ACCESS4ALL. “This raises a question for Brussels. When two equally capable lobbyists reach out to an EU policymaker about the same file, whose call gets returned?”

He added that one of the reasons why the Council might be “particularly challenging” to lobby is the “limited transparency surrounding its working parties, which makes it more difficult for lobbyists to identify who to approach on specific policy issues.”

The Council did not respond to a request for comment.

One lobbyist, Danijel Pantić, managing partner at the Brussels-based, Western Balkan-focused Eastern Bridge think tank, told Influence that the findings chimed with his experience.

The before times: He said some companies can get “indirect access” to an MEP through a political party. “But Commission services, that’s a fortress,” he said, adding: “We gave up.” He added: “Before Covid, it was possible. You’d send an email to somebody in the European Commission very transparently saying what you’d like to discuss. If they’re interested, they invite you, you have your 45 minutes and it was fine. Now it’s only possible through federations and associations.”

Even worse: He said this is particularly an issue for lobbyists from EU accession countries, arguing that EU policymakers only want to speak with them when there’s a big political moment in their countries. “It’s almost impossible to get access to the institutions if you’re making inquiries from accession countries,” he said. “Brussels is sacrificing this valuable feedback loop from those places.”

No issue: But another lobbyist from a Central European country that Influence spoke to (and who we’re keeping anonymous so he could speak freely) told us he was taken aback by the findings. “I was a bit surprised to be frank, I don’t really feel like I’m discriminated against because I’m from Central Europe,” he said. “I’m even more surprised that it’s the Council, because you have your country, and you have your network.” The lobbyist, who works at one of Brussels’ best-known consultancies, added that he speaks another Central European language and so is able to “lobby as if [that country] is my own.”

Perception: At the event Influence attended at which the research was presented (the full study will be made public in December), De Bruycker asked which countries might be over-represented in Brussels. Most agreed (to laughter) that it was probably Italy. But Finns, Dutch and Belgians are also particularly well-represented in Brussels, he pointed out.

Looking ahead: As for the numbers of people from Central and Eastern Europe entering the profession in Brussels, Marta Zoladz, a Polish-American public affairs specialist, reckons that’s about to shoot up. Speaking at the event in Etterbeek at which the research was delivered, she pointed out that the typical profile of a consultant in Brussels is someone with multiple languages and lots of travel under their belt. “To gain that experience … you certainly have to come from an economic background that allowed you to do that,” she said. “Speaking from my part of Europe, Central and Eastern Europe, I think you’re going to see more and more as the economic situation gets better. In Poland, people who grew up in the ’80s and ’90s didn’t have access to learning English.”

“Central and Eastern Europe is still not as represented as it should be compared with the West. Slowly but surely, I think this new generation — my generation, certainly — will participate more proactively as well,” said Zoladz.

Over to you: Does this resonate with any CEE consultants reading? Feel free to share your thoughts with Influence at meccles@politico.eu

UNCIVIL WAR

IT’S BEEN A WEEK: The center-right European People’s Party has repeatedly voted alongside the far-right in the Parliament (top colleagues Max Griera and Marianne Gros have the inside story on the potential political fallout for Roberta Metsola here). One area they’ve teamed up on is the future of EU funding for NGOs. EPP lawmakers sided with MEPs from the ECR and Patriots groups to approve a report that would bar NGOs from using EU funds for lobbying and advocacy — even though the report found that there’s no evidence the Commission paid groups to lobby.

But, but, but: The report, co-written by EPP lawmaker Dirk Gotink and ECR’s Carlo Fidanza, is the result of a year’s worth of work by the Scrutiny Working Group — a group of MEPs in the Parliament’s budgetary control committee tasked with looking into how the Commission awards funding to NGOs and other entities.

Lopsided: The group doesn’t include any MEPs left of the EPP — because Renew, the S&D, the Greens and the Left group are boycotting it. The report came about because conservative MEPs accused the Commission of paying environmental groups to lobby on its behalf in favor of the Green Deal. But their investigation found no “concrete proof ” that the Commission has been doing so or that any EU laws were broken.

No matter, say the MEPs, because they argue that EU money simply shouldn’t be used for NGO lobbying on principle. “The mere fact that the Commission and agencies approved and funded projects that included lobbying efforts appears, in itself, questionable,” the MEPs argue.

Cue NGO meltdown: Transparency International EU’s director Nick Aiossa called the report a “sham” produced by an “illegitimate” body. Ocean and fisheries campaigners BLOOM said the findings contradict the funding cuts they propose, warning NGOs would have to choose between resources and advocacy. WWF called the report “the culmination of a politically motivated campaign against civil society organisations.”

LOBBYING 101

HOW BIG OIL DEFEATED BRUSSELS: An op-ed for the Financial Times. A trip for MEPs to Texas. National companies lobbying their own ministries. And many, many, many meetings between fossil fuel execs and senior officials. All of these made up a lobbying masterclass delivered by Big Oil and the Trump administration that outwitted Brussels and delayed a climate law, our Ben Munster writes.

With a little help from the U.S: At the request of energy firms, U.S. officials got increasingly involved in the campaign, dispatching diplomats to member countries and issuing thundering denunciations of the regulation on social media. The complaints began to really gain traction with the intervention of senior officials from a Trump administration bent on a policy of “energy dominance” over Europe. U.S. Ambassador to the EU Andrew Puzder became the White House’s go-to critic of the rules in Brussels, weighing in regularly on social media and in media op-eds to call for a delay.

Transatlantic jaunt: The lobbying efforts even took one diverse group of MEPs all the way to Texas, where lawmakers were welcomed to the Houston HQ of LNG titan Cheniere and given a tour of ExxonMobil’s methane monitoring system. One MEP told POLITICO “that they had barely followed the file before embarking on the trip, but were left with the impression that serious supply disruptions could occur if a delay wasn’t introduced, and that oil and gas exporters may even stop selling to Europe to avoid non-compliance,” Ben writes.

Sponsored content: “The lawmaker added that they were also swayed to support a delay by an ExxonMobil ad that appeared in one of POLITICO’s newsletters.”

QUICK HITS

MEET THE ORBáNS: Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and his political director, Balázs Orbán (no relation), have founded a think tank called Pro Patria International Foundation. “We want to catalyze the debate on EU institutional reforms,” Balázs Orbán told Max Griera.

Who pays? “Fundraising will start now,” Orbán said, from “domestic and international donors.” They “don’t know yet” whether they will seek funding from the United States, as the White House made available millions of euros for conservative think tanks in Europe as part of its national security strategy.

Here in spirit: He added that the think tank will have “presence” in Brussels — but no office.

MANDELSON’S GLOBAL COUNSEL SHARES: Former EU Commissioner and British Labour grandee Peter Mandelson failed to sell his stake in his lobbying firm Global Counsel and attempted to influence No. 10 decisions after becoming ambassador to the U.S., according to a newly released tranche of documents relating to his appointment. Esther Webber writes that at the time of his appointment, Mandelson retained his shares in Global Counsel and that, despite having received an offer to buy them in March 2025, had failed to divest them six months later. The company collapsed in February 2026 after it lost a series of accounts amid coverage of Mandelson’s relationship with Jeffrey Epstein.

SIGNING ON: Good news for anyone who’s ever signed a European Citizens’ Initiative petition: the EU’s top court this week ruled that the European Commission must provide clear timetables for any action it intends to take in response to an ECI. It came after the Commission missed a four-year deadline to “end the cage age,” after 1.4 million EU citizens called for a ban on the use of cages for certain farmed animals.

INFLUENCERS

ENERGY

Marcell Sukosd-Kosa has started as EU affairs adviser at MOL Group. He was previously a consultant with PRM-CEE.

INSTITUTIONS

Michael Karnitschnig’s appointment as deputy director-general of DG ENEST has left staff at DG MENA wondering who’ll succeed him there as acting director-general. “Let the games begin,” one official told top colleague Gerardo Fortuna.

Florian Abadie has left the Greens in the European Parliament, and just joined DG COMP at the European Commission.

TECH & MEDIA

Ben Holles de Peyer has left DG COMP for Nvidia, where he’s now senior competition counsel in Brussels.

Giulia Iop has just started as head of European government affairs at Garmin, where she joins after several years with Sky.

Anne Duboscq, formerly at OVHcloud, has joined Eutelsat as chief communications officer.

Thanks to Max Griera, Annabelle Dickson, Ketrin Jochecová, Ben Munster, my editor Paul Dallison and producer Jo Shaw.

The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel

How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom

By Thomas Macaulay • 11.26.26

Hello!

Today: We meet the first person to take home a next-generation bionic hand that can feel, letting him hold fragile objects—and his wife's hand. Plus: Why AI's power demands rely so heavily on natural gas.

Psst: Our Cyber sale is happening now! Subscribe now and save 50% on year-long access to MIT Technology Review. You’ll also receive exclusive event session recordings and digital research reports on AI, energy, and climate tech.

The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel

Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he's cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it's wired up to nerves in his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, or a loved one's hand.

Davidson is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted, but he's the first to take it home and use it independently. Researchers hope his experiences will reveal how useful the technology really is in day-to-day life, and how it might affect his brain and nervous system.

Find out how a new generation of prosthetics is learning to feel.

—Jessica Hamzelou

How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom

—Casey Crownhart

In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote about how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I've lost count of how many times he's been proven right.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on have expanded, and the local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. Meanwhile, Meta's emissions are up 45% over last year's.

Across the US, natural gas has become the default to meet exploding power demand. Here’s what that means for the future of the grid.

This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 SpaceX has won approval to launch 1 million data center satellites

The FCC says they'll help meet AI computing demand. (Reuters $)

+ But they could overcrowd the orbit and obscure the stars. (Bloomberg $)

+ SpaceX must start deploying them by 2033 under its license. (BBC)

+ Europe has opened a megafactory to build a Starlink rival. (CNBC)

+ Can data centers really work in orbit? (MIT Technology Review)

2 The US Army has blown up nearly five tons of unstable explosives

The EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following the detonation. (Verge)

+ Scientists are now testing soil and water for contamination. (Wired $)

+ Officials were criticized for poor communication beforehand. (Axios)

3 Earth just had its first six-day streak above 2°C

Scientists say it’s an early warning of what's to come. (Guardian)

4 Ukraine has claimed the first-ever laser takedown of a jet drone

Its Blysk laser downed a Russian kamikaze drone. (Bloomberg $)

5 Neuralink has won approval for a brain-implant trial in ALS patients

It's the final stage of testing before seeking market clearance. (Gizmodo)

+ China is racing to catch up in brain-computer interfaces. (SCMP)

+ A BCI gave a man with ALS his voice back. (MIT Technology Review)

6 Hackers have breached the US Treasury's financial crime watchdog

It's taken systems used to report money laundering offline. (FT $)

7 Bankrupt startup Character.ai wants to sell millions of user chats

42 attorneys general are trying to block the sale. (TechCrunch)

8 The hunt for dark matter is getting weirder

Scientists are using levitating magnets and nuclear clocks. (Quanta)

+ Dark matter's hiding places keep growing. (MIT Technology Review)

9 Scientists used seabird spies to track ships that had gone dark

Recorders on the birds detected ships with trackers off. (404 Media)

10 This Thanksgiving, AI is becoming a popular sous-chef

But food bloggers say its recipes are often "total nonsense." (Axios)

Quote of the day

“Hey, by the way, this might be the last time we see each other—potentially, probably not, but maybe—because of AI.”

—Daniel Kokotajlo, former OpenAI researcher and author of the "AI 2027" forecast, tells The New York Times how he plans to bring up AI extinction risks with his wife’s family this Thanksgiving.

One more thing

AI models flub these intelligence tests. Can you fare any better?

Judged purely on its puzzling skills, AI is improving a lot—and quickly. In late 2024, even the best models could figure out only 18% of the infamous New York Times Connections puzzles; by early 2025, some could solve them nearly perfectly.

But puzzles do more than highlight AI's progress. Seeing where models succeed and fail, and where humans still beat them, offers a window into the technology's strengths and weaknesses.

We've gathered seven puzzles that have stumped models. Try them yourself to find out whether you can outsmart AI.

—Grace Huckins

Why do we need a new global order? What does the Putin-Xi-Trump summit in Shenzhen represent?

The Trump/Xi/Putin summit in Shenzhen is more than just a very unusual gathering of the three world leaders. It’s a manifestation of a broader shift in the international order: the end of the unipolar

Mastering Geopolitics

Nov 26

READ IN APP

Ricardo Martins, November 24, 2026

The Trump/Xi/Putin summit in Shenzhen is more than just a very unusual gathering of the three world leaders. It’s a manifestation of a broader shift in the international order: the end of the unipolar world that we’ve seen since the end of the Cold War with the US as the sole superpower, and the rise of a much more multipolar world in which Asia has become the central geopolitical arena.

The question is whether the three leaders are actually trying to create a new global order or whether they’re just managing the chaos that comes with the transition between the two competing international systems.

A new Yalta? The comparison was premature

The summit was compared to Yalta in 1945, when the “victor” powers were sitting down to work out the post-war order. That comparison is rather misleading, though. Yalta was in the context of total war, the complete collapse of the European powers and the occupation of vast parts of territory, which would go on to be the basis of the post-war division of Europe. Shenzhen is quite a different situation. It’s in a world of economic interdependence, a world of multiple regional powers and a very significant Global South.

Pledge your support

The Shenzhen summit didn’t create a new Yalta, and it certainly didn’t create a G3 that could run the world. Its real geopolitical significance is that it’s now widely accepted that global stability is going to require some form of accommodation between a number of power centres

As Sarang Shidore, director of the Global South Program at the Quincy Institute, points out, the symbolism of a great power concert is important, but the world we live in today is vastly more complex than the international system of 1945. The middle powers, the emerging economies and the non-Western institutions are not simply passive objects of the decisions of Washington, Moscow and Beijing.

Yet, the three leaders don’t have the same vision. Russia is in favour of a multipolar, polycentric world; China is pushing for multipolarity, development and greater representation for the Global South; the US is, of course, acknowledging that its former position of pre-eminence is no longer tenable and is still looking to gain strategic advantage and maintain its global position. The meeting is therefore not an agreement to divide the world into spheres of influence. It’s simply a recognition that the world is moving to a point where the interests of the great powers are increasingly converging, even if they are very different in nature.

What was achieved and what wasn’t?

The Joint Communiqué covered four main areas of agreement: reform of the UN, energy security, international criminal jurisdiction and nuclear risk reduction. As Pascal Lottaz from Neutrality Studies notes, the significance of the declaration from a political point of view was precisely that agreement between these three powers was by no means a foregone conclusion. It is, of course, a political declaration rather than a binding treaty.

The commitment to UN reform is a reflection of the frustration with institutions whose very structures are designed to perpetuate the distribution of power that emerged after the Second World War. The commitment to stable supplies and to refined products has implications for the world market and for the security of the energy-dependent economies. Nuclear risk reduction is undoubtedly the most important area of potential co-operation. The US, Russia and China all have the capability to affect the level of nuclear risk in the world, but declarations in themselves are not going to be sufficient. It is needed sustained negotiations, verification, and arms control agreements.

The narrowness of the communiqué should in no way be taken as evidence of irrelevance. Its value is in the fact that it has created a channel of communication between three strategic competitors at a time when the world is in a very volatile state. The fact that there is no actual agreement on Ukraine, Iran, Taiwan, trade or technology is testament to the extent of the divergence.

Share

China’s strategy: diplomacy, reassurance and strategic patience

Sheng Zhang‘s conversation with Pascal Lottaz in Neutrality Studies provides a very useful reading of China’s approach to diplomacy. The warmth Beijing has shown towards Trump (complete with all the symbolic gestures and personal diplomacy) is not to be taken as a sign of strategic surrender. The objective is to de-escalate tensions with Washington, to protect its space in the economic and technological spheres and to avoid any situation that could in the long run be detrimental to its development.

The summit thus serves as an example of managing the rivalry rather than resolving it. Beijing can give Trump the diplomatic recognition and the political symbolism that he wants, without in the slightest compromising its positions on Taiwan, on technology, on industrial policy and on its relationship with Russia. In that respect, the summit may well be a useful source of time for China.

Russia, on the other hand, is gaining by the very fact that Western sanctions have not rendered it diplomatically irrelevant. Putin’s presence at the event underlines Moscow’s continued status as a significant strategic player in the world, particularly in the areas of nuclear security and in Eurasia.

Trump’s involvement might just be a sign that the US simply can’t go on forever trying to manage every single regional conflict while at the same time containing China and dealing with Russia. A strategic recalibration doesn’t necessarily mean acceptance of a multipolar world. Recently in Athens, Secretary of State and Security Advisor Marco Rubio stated, “We don’t have a tripolar world. We have a unipolar world. The United States is the head of the world.” So, in Shenzhen, the US could be looking to negotiate from a position of strength rather than simply giving up on its hegemonic aspirations.

Europe, Latin America and the Global South

The implications for Europe are particularly stark. If the major international negotiations are increasingly being conducted outside of the European diplomatic framework, then the EU will be a strategic observer. Its own fragmentation, its dependence on American security guarantees and its lack of capacity to act independently — all work against Europe. The summit should therefore be a wake-up call. European strategic autonomy requires political unity, credible defence capabilities and a capable and independent diplomatic capability. It doesn’t require simply a declaration of unity.

For Latin America, the new order could well create more scope for manoeuvre. The US-China rivalry coupled with Russia’s continued international activity could open up new possibilities for economic partnerships, infrastructure investment and diplomatic diversification. The catch is of course that multipolarity doesn’t necessarily equate to sovereignty. A country that seeks to diversify its partnerships without concomitant investment in its own institutions, its own industrial base and its regional cooperation may simply be substituting one dependency for another.

For the wider Global South, the real issue isn’t so much about replacing the West with Chinese or Russian dominance (though that might be an outcome in some cases) but about getting a greater degree of representation in global governance, access to development finance, access to technology, fairer terms of trade and respect for national sovereignty.

Beyond unipolarity: the need for a new global order

The Shenzhen summit didn’t create a new Yalta, and it certainly didn’t create a G3 that could run the world. Its real geopolitical significance is that it’s now widely accepted that global stability is going to require some form of accommodation between a number of power centres.

The unipolar world is over. The geopolitical centre of gravity has moved to Asia, and Trump clearly sees, despite certain falcons in Washington, such as Marco Rubio, that the US has to adjust to that reality. The transition is still dangerous though as the old institutions are losing credibility, the new arrangements are still in their infancy, and the competition is still there.

A genuinely sustainable global order can’t just be one that reflects the interests of the most powerful states. It has to also take into account the aspirations of the middle powers, the regional organisations and the Global South. The issue isn’t simply one of redistributing power but of creating institutions that can deal with interdependence, that can prevent war and that can deliver on development. That’s why we need a new global order, and that’s why the Shenzhen summit (however little it achieved in terms of tangible outcomes) may well be a significant moment in the wider debate about what comes next.

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

AI & THE HOLIDAYS

🦃 Your AI cheat sheet for Thanksgiving dinner

Image source: Images 2.6 / The Rundown

The Rundown: AI is probably going to come up in discussion around the table during the holidays, and this month provided plenty of material. Here’s your cheat sheet for some of the questions most likely to get dished out, with explanations to help you feel like the AI expert in the room.

Q: What’s going on with Nvidia and Jensen Huang? Was he really having an affair with a spy?

A: Jensen was out, and now he’s back, with some lobbying from the President playing a role. Nvidia’s stock saw $1T in value added on his return, and lawmakers are furious — and ready to hold his feet to the fire in hearings starting on Dec. 3.

As for his affair with Alice Huang, her spy ties are looking less clear by the day. Despite early reporting, U.S. officials reportedly have no proof she was told to pry secrets from Jensen, though she was in touch with Chinese intelligence. The bigger issue is chips: investigators suspect her old firm Megaspeed helped Nvidia hardware slip into China, and the U.S. blacklisted it Monday.

Q: Why does it feel like everything’s getting hacked or breaking lately? Is AI to blame?

A: Sort of — but it’s also the solution. AI is now extremely adept at finding bugs that sat unnoticed in everyday software for a decade or more. The code behind much of the web, including critical software and infrastructure, is not as safe as we once thought, and defenders are racing (with their own AI) to find and patch the holes.

Unfortunately, expect more chaos, as more AI-exposed vulnerabilities seem inevitable at this point.

Q: Did AI really solve some famous math problem?

A: Yes, many of them. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and others are all letting AI loose on the math world, solving open problems in the field left and right and igniting a firestorm between mathematicians and the AI labs.

The biggest: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge claimed last week that he and Claude solved the Riemann Hypothesis, a $1M Millennium Prize problem considered the most famous open problem in mathematics. Also historic was OpenAI's Navier-Stokes solution in September and its release of 700+ AI-written math papers in October.

NATE’S NOTEBOOK

🪙 What five cents builds now with AI

The Rundown: Each week, Rundown AI educator Nate Grahek breaks down what he's seeing while teaching real teams to use AI.

Nate: Live sports is the one place we all still sit through loud, annoying ads. My wife yells, “God, turn it down,” and I’m digging for the remote. One Saturday, it hit me: I could take a picture every second of what’s on my TV. If my Mac could look at each one and answer one question — game or ad — the TV could mute itself.

My brain said no way. I ran a software company for photographers, and we hosted terabytes of their images. A freeze frame every second of a three-hour game? I figured $10 or $20 a game, fine for a funny proof of concept.

It took under 30 minutes to build. It was 95% accurate on the first try. The cost? 5 cents a game.

Then the snowball started. Once it could mute the ads, I thought about what I do during them: grab my phone and scroll for funny posts to send my buddies. So those went up on the TV. Then I swapped my feed for agents reading the top channels across every network, putting the best 20 posts on screen for the whole family to laugh at. I even swapped the TV announcers for the radio broadcast.

Advertisers are not ready for this.

My experience is my biggest asset, and it’s also my biggest blind spot: I keep assuming complexity and costs that aren’t there. Before you scope version one of anything, ask AI, “What am I assuming is too hard or too expensive to try?”

Developers, I get it: you don’t have the freedom to experiment at work. So pick a silly, almost disposable project and spend $200 blowing through a Fable limit this weekend just to see what happens.

AI TRAINING

🏷️ Check Black Friday prices with Gemini Tasks

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll use Tasks in Gemini to check the price of one thing you want to buy this Black Friday week. Gemini compares six stores in one table, looks into whether the discount is real, and checks again every day until a date you choose.

Step-by-step:

Go to Gemini on the web or app, sign in with your personal Google Account, and select Task. If you can choose a model, pick Hydrogen, the one free accounts use

Paste the guide's price prompt with your own product and stores, and keep limits: “Use web search only, not this computer or my browser,” no sign-in or purchase

Open the lowest link, then the lowest one where the store itself is the seller. Check the model, that it's new, who sells it, the price with shipping, and the return window

In the same chat, ask: “Is [price] a real discount? Tell me the list price, the lowest price you can find evidence for before this month, and where each number comes from. Use web search only”

If you can wait, ask Gemini to check the same stores every day until December 1 and to tell you only if the price drops below yours

Pro tip: Put your limits in the first message: the exact model, which stores, who must be the seller, and what Gemini must not touch. Then open the store's page before you pay.

DARIO AMODEI

✍️ Anthropic CEO claps back at Axios ‘free will’ report

Image source: Dario Amodei on X

The Rundown: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei responded to an Axios report tying him and his staff to the idea of letting superintelligent AI make some of humanity's decisions, calling it “absurd” and accusing rivals of “vibes-based” positioning on human control.

The details:

Axios said some Anthropic staffers back letting superintelligent AI make certain decisions, also pointing to an old slide pitching a “utopia ruled by god in a box.”

Meta's Alexandr Wang publicly rejected a “handover” to AI, and Sam Altman said this month that he wants people “to have the agency over the future.”

Amodei answered on X that turning governance over to AI is a “terrible idea,” comparing it to trading democracy for the speed autocrats promise.

He also said rivals touting “human control and agency” sell similar tools, while only Anthropic has taken a stand on issues like autonomous weapons use.

Why it matters: Anthropic has long paired its safety-first reputation with treating Claude as more than a tool, so it's no shock that some staff are open to AI taking over certain decisions, whatever Amodei says. Insiders could be sounding an alarm over that view, but they've also handed rivals a headline-grabbing talking point against the AI leader.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Ben built an accessibility gatekeeper for Claude Code

Today’s workflow comes from reader Ben McOsker:

“I built a workflow that turns my brand's colors and fonts into website building blocks that people using screen readers, keyboards, larger text, or high contrast can use with ease. AI does the building, and an automated checker decides whether the work ships.

Before anything is built, Claude writes a short brief. Claude Code builds from the brief, the way a contractor builds from blueprints. Automated checks run every time Claude finishes something, before I look at it. If anything fails, the work is blocked. Claude gets a report showing exactly what failed and why. It fixes the problem and submits again. Only work that passes every check gets in. There's no override button, not even for me.

The result is a free, open-source tool. Give it your brand's colors and fonts, and it produces 18 ready-to-use building blocks, each accessibility-checked and shown in a live showroom with instructions.”

UNITED STATES. Over it

New 'overcapacity' tariffs hit as inflation rises.

The Trump administration said new levies of between 20% and 40% could be “actionable” on 14 trade partners, including China, under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The US Trade Representative said hearings would be held in January.

INTELLIGENCE. Like with 2025’s “Liberation Day”, the proposed duties are a cudgel, ahead of further horse-trading, but markets nonetheless fell sharply on the news. Claims of “industrial overcapacity”, always rubbery at best, need not be definitely proven under the Trade Act’s authority, but they’ll at least give Americans something else to talk about at Thanksgiving, other than Iran, AI and grounded flights. Trump blamed the Democrats for the market’s rout.

FOR BUSINESS. The proposed tariffs are on China, the EU, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India. Mexico and Norway may receive their own soon. The merits are as debatable as any of the administration’s previous policies, but show the trade war isn’t over, even with personal consumption expenditures inflation at 3.8% and an almost guaranteed rate hike in December.

😺 Anthropic's CEO Rejects the Idea of AI Governing Society

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said Wednesday that humans should not hand society's big decisions over to AI. He was answering an Axios report about a split among AI leaders. Citing people familiar with company discussions, Axios said a common view inside Anthropic holds that humanity will eventually cede some decision-making power to superintelligent AI, and that rival executives are pushing back.

His reply was blunt. He called the idea that he wants humans to surrender free will absurd, and said AI should be governed through legitimate democratic processes. Nothing says "that landed" like answering a news story with an essay.

The useful part is the line he drew between two things that sound alike. Letting AI do a task is one thing. Letting AI write the rules everyone lives under is another. Think Roomba versus mayor.

Here's what he said:

Tasks. His view is mixed, since AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end to end can be clearly desirable and save lives.

Pace. It may make sense to slow or stop some deployments, to limit job disruption and AI's ability to build more powerful AI on its own.

The timing matters. Axios reported a day earlier that employees at Anthropic and OpenAI privately worry some unreleased models are too powerful to release safely, which we covered yesterday. And in August, Amodei pushed back on an investor's claim that Anthropic wants to be the last private company standing.

Our take: An AI-run society sounds like sci-fi, and we won't pretend it's impossible. AI keeps taking over work that used to need a person, and that trajectory points toward systems as smart as us, or smarter. Still, we don't think handing over the keys makes the best society.

We humans are a mess. We make mistakes, we repeat them, and sometimes we wreck the very things we love. But the same species shows up at 2 a.m. for a sick friend, forgives people who don't deserve it, and builds things for strangers it will never meet. Our flaws and our goodness come as a package, and we wouldn't trade the second to fix the first. Democratic processes are how flawed people have always governed themselves, because we can argue, vote, and fix our mistakes, and that's the part we don't want to hand over.

That's where we land with Pope Leo XIV's Magnifica Humanitas, which we covered in May, and its call to go back to humanity. AI can do remarkable things, and we want people to thrive because of it. A world where AI advances on the back of our flaws has it backwards. The line worth watching is where each lab says a task ends and a decision about how people live begins.

🎓 AI Skill of the Day: Make your coding agent prove every speedup

Ask a coding agent to make slow code faster and it will happily hand you a confident rewrite. Whether the rewrite is actually faster, or still correct, is a separate question. Heidelberg University's Algorithm Engineering Group built Agentic Algorithm Engineering, an MIT-licensed skill for Claude Code and Codex, to force that question.

Before the agent touches anything, you agree on four things with it. Those are the benchmark, the metric, the correctness checks (for example, output that must be bit-identical), and a budget. Then it works in loops built around a falsifiable hypothesis, which is a prediction you can prove wrong.

State the prediction, such as "this change should cut runtime by roughly this much, for this reason."

Estimate the size of the effect from profiling before measuring anything.

Make one small change, commit it to Git, and run the correctness checks.

Run the benchmark, and keep the change only if it's faster and still correct. Otherwise it gets reverted.

In the project's example session on the KaHIP graph partitioner, the agent ran 122 experiments, tested 69 hypotheses, kept 41 patches, and finished 3.9x faster. On another tool, VieCut, it reported 8.9x with every result unchanged. A confident explanation is not a benchmark.

To try it in Claude Code, run /plugin install aae --marketplace CHSZLab/AgenticAlgorithmEngineering, then /aae:aae followed by your task. No Claude Code? Borrow the habit with this prompt, which is our own adaptation and not from the project.

Here is the slow task and a representative input: [details]. Propose one change and explain why it might help. Give me a repeatable before-and-after measurement and a correctness check. Do not claim improvement until the tests have run.

New publication: The flawed story of pragmatic retrenchment – What Europe can learn from Spain’s sustained ambition

This policy brief by Jannik Jansen shows that Spain’s sustained ambition on climate, industry, and migration has helped drive stronger economic performance than many of its European peers.͏ ͏ ͏ ͏ ͏ ͏ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­ ­

Dear Readers,

Fears of deindustrialisation and decline have taken a firm hold across Europe. As slowing the green transition, scaling back industrial policy, and tightening migration are cast as a return to pragmatic realism, Spain has taken the opposite course on all three counts, yet has outpaced the EU's other large economies.

In his new policy brief, our Senior Policy Fellow Jannik Jansen traces how cheap clean power, investment into strategic value chains, and legal migration pathways have contributed to that performance.

Some of the favourable conditions Spain has enjoyed cannot be replicated and its record is not without gaps, he argues. Spain's experience, however, suggests that sustained ambition is the more pragmatic course for governments seeking to restore economic strength.

You can find the full policy brief "The flawed story of pragmatic retrenchment – What Europe can learn from Spain’s sustained ambition" by Jannik Jansen on our website. For further questions, please contact our Press and PR Office.

Renault Filante targets drivers sensitive to ride comfort

Renault Filante targets drivers sensitive to ride comfort. For some drivers, ride comfort is decided by the smallest details — a bump over a speed hump, a manhole cover or a seam in the road. These minor impacts may go unnoticed at first, but once drivers become sensitive to them, they can become a constant part of the driving experience. Unlike horsepower or fuel economy, ride comfort is difficult to capture in a specification sheet. It depends on how a vehicle responds to different road surfaces and how effectively it keeps vibrations and noise away from occupants. Renault Korea’s flagship Filante crossover is designed around this everyday driving experience, with a focus on balancing comfort and stability across a wide range of road conditions. A key part of the setup is its frequency-sensitive damper, which is fitted as standard across the lineup. The system adjusts damping characteristics according to the frequency of vibrations generated by the road. NYT Warns Photographers Not To Update Photoshop Over AI Features

NYT Warns Photographers Not To Update Photoshop Over AI Features. The New York Times is instructing freelance photographers not to use Adobe Photoshop 2027 (version 28.0.0 and subsequent updates), warning that its new AI features operate "in ways that may not be apparent to users" and "can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated." The Verge reports: It's not always clear which tools in Adobe's apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers' trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not "retouch or digitally manipulate" photos but may "make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image." In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. of this story at Slashdot. .

Anthropic Created a Honeypot To Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving. An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren, a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures. The test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sits just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that's cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps. [. ] Earlier versions of Claude are much more likely to fall into the honeypot trap than newer models, according to test runs with Siren. The more recent models have been given additional training designed to make them less likely to break the rules when performing agentic tasks. "We've added this in both our supervised learning sets and a few reinforcement learning environments," says Oscar O'Rahilly, an Anthropic researcher who specializes in AI training and who helped develop Siren. "This could be a driving factor for why it has improved so much." O'Rahilly says that models reason about whether to give in to temptation, which may partly explain why smarter models are less likely to break bad. Siren experiments also showed that giving Claude a simple additional piece of text explaining that it should not escape the sandbox resulted in drastically fewer efforts to break free. In Anthropic's tests, Claude 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.2 fell for the honeypot between 0.6 and 1.6 percent of the time. Two earlier models, Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5, went rogue 12.7 percent and 25.8 percent of the time, respectively. AI models are sometimes known to behave better if they know they're being tested. But O'Rahilly says other experiments suggest that Claude actually behaves more responsibly if it thinks a scenario is real rather than a test. As AI models get ever smarter, many researchers worry about whether they'll outwit their human counterparts. If that does happen, then it may be essential that agents -- and not just the executives responsible for them -- can resist temptation. of this story at Slashdot. .

New York Bans AI Toys For 5 Years

New York Bans AI Toys For 5 Years. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed legislation Tuesday banning the manufacture, exchange, distribution and sale of toys powered by AI chatbots for five years. "The law will take effect 90 days after signing, meaning the restrictions will not be in place during this year's holiday shopping season," reports FOX Chattanooga. "In the meantime, Hochul is encouraging parents and caregivers to consider potential safety and privacy risks before purchasing AI-powered toys for children." From the report: The legislation, S.9408A/A.11144B, applies to toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, including talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with children. [. ] Under the new law, violators could face civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day for each violation, with enforcement handled by the New York Attorney General's Office. State Sen. Andrew Gounardes said the five-year moratorium will provide time to study the technology's impact on children and develop additional safety protections. of this story at Slashdot. .
